units.title: Unit 1: Basic Economic Concepts
units.body:
Overview
Basic Economic Concepts

Core ideas
- Scarcity forces every society to make choices, and every choice carries an opportunity cost.
- PPC logic helps you classify efficient, inefficient, and unattainable outcomes while showing tradeoffs and growth.
- Comparative advantage is about lower opportunity cost, not higher total output.

Topics
- Comparative and Absolute Advantage
- Opportunity Cost and Trade-Offs
- Specialization and Gains from Trade
- Economic Systems and Resource Allocation
- PPC and Opportunity Cost
- Scarcity, Choice, and Opportunity Cost

Key vocab
- Absolute Advantage
- Capital
- Command Economy
- Comparative Advantage
- Economic System
- Efficient
- Entrepreneurship
- Factors of Production
- Gains from Trade
- Incentives
- Inefficient
- Labor
- Land
- Marginal Analysis

Common mistakes
- Confusing comparative advantage with absolute advantage.
- Calling a point inside the PPC unattainable instead of inefficient.
- Forgetting that opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up.

Exam reminders
- Ask: efficient, inefficient, or unattainable?
- Ask: which producer has the lower opportunity cost?
- If resources or technology improve, the PPC shifts outward.

Supply and Demand

Core ideas
- Market equilibrium is the baseline for almost every AP Micro policy graph.
- Know the difference between a shift of a curve and a movement along a curve.
- Elasticity explains how responsive buyers or sellers are, and it drives tax incidence and total revenue logic.

Common mistakes

- Using the starting quantity instead of the midpoint average in elasticity calculations.
- Assuming the side that legally pays the tax always bears the burden.

Exam reminders

- Elastic demand means quantity responds more than price.
- In a tax graph, use post-tax quantity for the rectangle and triangle.

units.title: Unit 3: Production, Cost, and Perfect Competition
units.body:
Overview
Production, Cost, and Perfect Competition

Core ideas
- Production and cost curves connect marginal product, marginal cost, and firm behavior.
- In perfect competition, firms are price takers and the profit-max rule is still MR = MC.
- Short-run shutdown and long-run exit decisions depend on comparing price with AVC and ATC.

Common mistakes
- Mixing up fixed cost changes with marginal cost changes.
- Using ATC instead of AVC for the shutdown rule.
- Forgetting that MC crosses AVC and ATC at their minimum points.

Exam reminders
- Diminishing marginal returns pushes MC up.
- Perfectly competitive firms have horizontal demand = MR = AR = price.
- Economic profit can be zero in long-run equilibrium without meaning the firm leaves.

Imperfect Competition

Core ideas
- Imperfect competitors face downward-sloping demand, so price is above marginal revenue.
- Monopoly and oligopoly questions often combine graph reading, profit rectangles, and efficiency analysis.
- For monopoly, MR = MC gives quantity first; price is read from demand.

- Monopolistic competition earns zero economic profit in the long run but still has excess capacity.
- Oligopoly questions often turn on strategic incentives and Nash equilibrium.

units.title: Unit 5: Factor Markets
units.body:
Overview
Factor Markets

Core ideas
- Factor markets apply the same optimizing logic to labor and other inputs.
- In a competitive labor market, firms hire workers until MRP equals the wage rate.
- Monopsony uses MFC above labor supply, which reduces wages and employment relative to competition.

Topics

Common mistakes
- Using total revenue instead of marginal revenue product.
- Forgetting that labor demand is downward sloping because of diminishing marginal product.
- Missing the distinction between competitive hiring and monopsony hiring.

Exam reminders
- Hire inputs where marginal benefit equals marginal cost.
- For labor, that rule is MRP = wage in a competitive labor market.
- Monopsony hires less and pays less than a competitive labor market.

units.title: Unit 6: Market Failure and the Role of Government
units.body:
Overview
Market Failure and the Role of Government

Core ideas
- Externalities, public goods, and common resources explain why private markets can miss the socially efficient outcome.
- Unit 6 hinges on first-class social-cost and social-benefit language: MPC, MSC, MPB, MSB, and the socially optimal quantity.
- Government tools such as corrective taxes, subsidies, regulation, and public provision aim to move output toward MSB = MSC.

Topics
- Externalities and Socially Efficient Output
- Negative Externalities
- Positive Externalities
- Government Intervention and Corrective Policy
- Public Goods
- Common Resources
- Free Rider Problem
- Inequality, Lorenz Curve, and Gini
- Public Goods and Common Resources

Key vocab
- Common Resource
- Corrective Tax
- Cost-Benefit Analysis
- Deadweight Loss
- Externality
- Free Rider
- Free Rider Problem
- Gini Coefficient
- Lorenz Curve
- Marginal External Benefit
- Marginal External Cost
- MPB
- MPC
- MSB

Common mistakes
- Treating the market equilibrium as socially efficient when MPC differs from MSC or MPB differs from MSB.
- Mixing up non-rival with non-excludable or confusing a public good with a common resource.
- Naming a policy tool without explaining how it moves quantity toward the socially optimal quantity.

Exam reminders
- Social optimum is where MSB = MSC, not where private-market curves alone intersect.
- Negative externalities mean MSC > MPC and overproduction; positive externalities mean MSB > MPB and underproduction.
- Public goods are underprovided because of free riders; common resources are overused because users ignore the external cost of depletion.

topics.title: Comparative and Absolute Advantage
topics.body:
Comparative advantage depends on lower opportunity cost, while absolute advantage depends on greater output. Specialization and trade let both sides move beyond what they could consume on their own.

Key ideas
- Comparative advantage depends on lower opportunity cost, while absolute advantage depends on higher total output.
- A producer should specialize in the good for which it has the lower opportunity cost even if it has an absolute advantage in both goods.
- Mutually beneficial trade is possible when the terms of trade fall between the two producers' opportunity costs.

Key vocabulary

- Comparative Advantage

topics.title: Opportunity Cost and Trade-Offs
topics.body:
Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up when a decision is made. AP Micro uses it to read PPC trade-offs, identify comparative advantage, and explain rational economic choice.

Key ideas
- Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up when a decision is made.
- On a PPC, opportunity cost is read from the trade-off between the two goods, often using the slope or output sacrifice.
- Comparative advantage depends on lower opportunity cost, not on who can produce the most total output.

Graphs to review

Key vocabulary

topics.title: Specialization and Gains from Trade
topics.body:
Specialization and trade let producers focus on what they do relatively best, then exchange for combinations that would be harder or impossible to reach alone. Gains from trade come from comparative advantage and favorable terms of trade.

Key ideas
- Specialization means focusing production on the good with the lowest opportunity cost.
- Trade creates gains because specialization lets both sides consume combinations that are better than what they could reach alone.
- AP Micro trade questions usually ask who specializes in what, who trades for what, and why both sides benefit.

Graphs to review

topics.title: Economic Systems and Resource Allocation
topics.body:
Economic systems answer what to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce. AP Micro mostly emphasizes market allocation, incentives, and the role of prices in coordinating choices.

Key ideas
- Economic systems answer what to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce.
- Market economies rely on prices, incentives, and private property, while command economies rely more on central planning and government direction.
- Most real economies are mixed economies that combine markets with government rules, taxes, transfers, and public goods.

topics.title: PPC and Opportunity Cost
topics.body:
A production possibilities curve shows the maximum output combinations of two goods that can be produced with current resources and technology. Use it to classify efficient, inefficient, and unattainable points and to measure opportunity cost.

Key ideas
- Points on the PPC are productively efficient because all available resources are fully employed.
- Points inside the PPC are inefficient because some resources are idle or misused, while points outside are unattainable with current resources and technology.
- An outward shift of the PPC shows economic growth from more resources, better technology, or improved productivity.
- How is economic growth shown on a PPC? If however, the technology only affects the production of one of the goods it will look like this Kebabs PIZZA Kebabs PIZZA

topics.title: Scarcity, Choice, and Opportunity Cost
topics.body:
Economics starts with scarcity: resources are limited, so individuals and societies must choose. Every choice has an opportunity cost, and rational decision-making compares marginal benefit with marginal cost.

Key ideas
- Scarcity forces all people and societies to make choices because resources are limited while wants are unlimited.
- Every choice creates a trade-off because choosing one option means giving up another option.
- AP Micro often frames rational choice as comparing marginal benefit with marginal cost or opportunity cost.
- Cost-Benefit Analysis 1.5Marginal Analysis and Consumer Choice 1.6
- Economic profit goes further by including implicit costs - the opportunities you gave up by making this choice.

- The per-unit subsidy reduces the marginal cost, which increases the quantity produced and moves production closer to the allocatively efficient output

topics.title: Monopolistic Competition
topics.body:
Monopolistic competition combines many firms with differentiated products and low barriers to entry. Firms have some pricing power, but entry erodes economic profit in the long run and leaves excess capacity.

Key ideas
- Product differentiation gives each firm a downward-sloping demand curve and some price-setting power.
- In the short run, the firm uses MR = MC for output and demand for price just like other imperfect competitors.
- In the long run, entry shifts demand left until price equals ATC, leaving zero economic profit but excess capacity.

- Oligopoly is defined by interdependence, so each firm's decision depends on expected rival reactions.
- Game theory is used because firms must think strategically instead of taking the market as given.

- Collusion means firms coordinate to restrict output or raise price in order to earn higher joint profit.
- A cartel tries to imitate the monopoly outcome, which increases profit but reduces consumer welfare.

- A dominant strategy is the best action regardless of what the rival chooses.

topics.title: Profit Maximization in Imperfect Competition
topics.body:
Imperfectly competitive firms still use marginal analysis: choose output where MR = MC, then use the demand curve to read price. The key AP trap is that MR = MC gives quantity first, not price.

Key ideas
- For monopoly and monopolistic competition, MR lies below demand because lowering price on the last unit affects earlier units too.
- The firm finds the profit-maximizing quantity where MR = MC.
- Only after choosing quantity does the firm move up to demand to read price.

topics.title: Efficiency and Consumer Impact in Imperfect Competition
topics.body:
Imperfect competition usually fails to achieve allocative and productive efficiency. Monopoly and monopolistic competition produce where price exceeds marginal cost, and monopolistic competition also operates with excess capacity.

Key ideas
- Allocative efficiency requires P = MC, but monopoly and monopolistic competition usually produce where P > MC.
- Productive efficiency requires output at minimum ATC, but monopolistic competition produces to the left of that point.
- Deadweight loss appears when firms restrict output below the efficient level.

topics.title: Factor Markets
topics.body:
Factor markets apply marginal analysis to inputs such as labor, land, and capital. The central AP comparison is between a competitive labor market, where wage and employment are set by supply and demand, and monopsony, where a single buyer hires less labor and pays a lower wage.

Key ideas
- Factor markets use the same marginal logic as product markets, but the choice is how much input to hire instead of how much output to produce.
- Competitive labor markets set wage and employment at the intersection of labor demand and labor supply.
- Monopsony sets employment where MRP = MFC and then pays the wage on the labor-supply curve at that quantity.

topics.title: Derived Demand and Input Demand
topics.body:
Demand for labor is derived from demand for the output labor helps produce. If consumers want more of the final product or workers become more productive, the marginal revenue product of labor rises and firms demand more labor.

Key ideas
- Firms do not want labor for its own sake; they want labor because workers help produce something buyers want.
- Higher demand for the final product raises MR or price, which raises MRP and shifts labor demand to the right.
- Higher worker productivity also shifts labor demand right because each worker adds more output.

topics.title: MRP, MRC, and Hiring Rule
topics.body:
A firm hires labor up to the point where the extra benefit from the last worker equals the extra cost of hiring that worker. In a competitive labor market, that rule is MRP = wage because wage is the firm's marginal resource cost.

Key ideas
- MRP is the marginal benefit of one more worker, while MRC is the marginal cost of that worker.
- If MRP exceeds MRC, hiring another worker raises profit; if MRP is below MRC, the firm should cut back.
- The profit-maximizing quantity of labor is where the two are equal.

topics.title: Competitive Labor Market
topics.body:
A competitive labor market sets the equilibrium wage and quantity of labor where labor demand intersects labor supply. Individual firms take the wage as given, so they can hire as much labor as they want at that market wage.

Key ideas
- A competitive labor market has many firms hiring labor and many workers supplying labor.
- The equilibrium wage is the wage where labor demand equals labor supply.
- Each individual firm is a wage taker even though the market wage is set by supply and demand.

topics.title: Wage Determination
topics.body:
Wages are determined by both the demand for labor and the supply of labor. Changes in productivity, product demand, worker preferences, education, migration, and population can all shift labor-market outcomes.

Key ideas
- Wages rise when labor demand shifts right or labor supply shifts left.
- Wages fall when labor demand shifts left or labor supply shifts right.
- AP explanations should always identify which side of the labor market changed and why.

topics.title: Labor Market Equilibrium
topics.body:
Labor-market equilibrium is the wage and employment outcome where the quantity of labor demanded equals the quantity of labor supplied. AP questions often compare this competitive benchmark with a monopsony outcome or a shifted labor-demand curve.

Key ideas
- Equilibrium wage is read on the vertical axis and equilibrium quantity of labor is read on the horizontal axis.
- At equilibrium there is no labor shortage or labor surplus.
- This competitive outcome is the benchmark for comparing monopsony or policy interventions.

topics.title: Resource Demand Shifters
topics.body:
Resource demand shifts when the marginal revenue product of an input changes. Productivity changes, output-price changes, or changes in the prices of complementary resources can all shift labor demand.

Key ideas
- Output demand rises -> labor demand rises because each worker helps produce a more valuable product.
- Worker productivity rises -> labor demand rises because each worker adds more output.
- The price of a complementary resource falling can also raise labor demand if the two inputs work better together.

topics.title: Resource Supply Shifters
topics.body:
Resource supply shifts when workers' willingness to offer labor changes. Changes in preferences, the size or training of the labor force, migration, and alternative job opportunities can shift labor supply.

Key ideas
- More trained workers, immigration, or population growth can shift labor supply right.
- Better nonwage job conditions elsewhere or stronger preferences for leisure can shift labor supply left.
- Always separate supply-side worker decisions from demand-side firm decisions.

topics.title: Labor Markets, MRP, and Hiring
topics.body:
Factor-market labor questions ask how many workers a firm should hire and what determines labor demand. In competitive hiring, firms treat the wage as marginal resource cost and hire labor until marginal revenue product equals wage.

Key ideas
- Labor demand is the firm's MRP curve, so it slopes downward because marginal product eventually falls.
- In a perfectly competitive labor market, each firm treats the wage as fixed and hires where MRP = wage.
- If the price of the firm's output rises, the MRP curve shifts right because each worker now brings in more revenue.
- i. MRP=MFC or MRP=Wage or MRP=MRC. ii.
- Definition: the additional revenue from hiring an additional worker MRP=MP x MR or MRP=MP x P

topics.title: Externalities and Socially Efficient Output
topics.body:
Externalities create a gap between private and social outcomes. The socially efficient quantity occurs where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost, not where private curves alone intersect.

Key ideas
- Externalities create a wedge between private incentives and social efficiency because some costs or benefits spill onto third parties.
- The socially optimal quantity is found where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost, not where the private market settles.
- AP often tests whether the market overproduces, underproduces, and which policy tool could move output toward the efficient level.
- 6.1 Socially Efficient and Inefficient Market Outcomes & 6.2 Externalities

topics.title: Negative Externalities
topics.body:
Negative externalities create external costs, so marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost and the market overproduces relative to the socially optimal quantity.

Key ideas
- Negative externalities create external costs, so MSC lies above MPC and the market quantity is too high.
- The private market ignores some of the full social cost, which creates deadweight loss from overproduction.
- A corrective tax or strong regulation can reduce quantity toward the socially optimal quantity.

topics.title: Positive Externalities
topics.body:
Positive externalities create external benefits, so marginal social benefit exceeds marginal private benefit and the market underproduces relative to the socially optimal quantity.

Key ideas
- Positive externalities create external benefits, so MSB lies above MPB and the market quantity is too low.
- The private market ignores some of the full social benefit, which creates deadweight loss from underproduction.
- A subsidy, public provision, or direct support can raise quantity toward the socially optimal quantity.

topics.title: Government Intervention and Corrective Policy
topics.body:
Corrective policy uses taxes, subsidies, regulation, permits, or public provision to move output toward the socially efficient outcome when private incentives diverge from social costs or benefits.

Key ideas
- Corrective policy aims to internalize an external cost or benefit so the market outcome moves closer to MSB = MSC.
- Corrective taxes work best for negative externalities, while subsidies work best for positive externalities.
- Regulation, permits, quotas, and public provision are also valid AP policy tools when prices alone are not enough.

topics.title: Public Goods
topics.body:
Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable, so private markets tend to underprovide them because consumers can benefit without paying.

Key ideas
- Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable, so one person's use does not reduce another person's use and nonpayers are hard to exclude.
- Because consumers can free ride, private firms struggle to capture enough revenue and the market underprovides the good.
- Government often funds or directly provides public goods such as national defense or street lighting.

topics.title: Common Resources
topics.body:
Common resources are rival and non-excludable, so individuals tend to overuse them because each user ignores the depletion cost imposed on others.

Key ideas
- Common resources are rival and non-excludable, so each person's use leaves less for others.
- Because access is open, individuals ignore the depletion cost imposed on others and overuse the resource.
- Property rights, quotas, permits, and regulation can reduce the tragedy of the commons.

topics.title: Free Rider Problem
topics.body:
The free-rider problem occurs when people benefit from a good without paying for it, which helps explain why private markets underprovide public goods.

Key ideas
- A free rider receives the benefit of a good or service without paying for it.
- Free riding weakens the market signal for public goods because private demand understates the full social benefit.
- AP often uses free-rider logic to explain why government provision or taxation may be necessary.

topics.title: Inequality, Lorenz Curve, and Gini
topics.body:
Lorenz curves and the Gini coefficient summarize how evenly income is distributed. The farther the Lorenz curve bends away from the equality line, the greater the inequality.

Key ideas
- How do we measure income inequality?
- The Lorenz Curve The Lorenz Curve shows the percentage of all income received by the poorest members of the population, from the poorest 0% to the poorest 100%

vocabulary.related_terms: Labor Demand, Derived Demand, Marginal Revenue Product
vocabulary.confusion: Watch for similar-looking graph labels and AP wording traps.
vocabulary.exam_tip: It is the firm's willingness to hire labor at different wages.

vocabulary.short_definition: Demand for an input that comes from the demand for the final good or service the input helps produce.
vocabulary.long_definition: Demand for an input that comes from the demand for the final good or service the input helps produce. Labor is demanded because workers help produce output that firms can sell. On AP graphs it appears as a curve located Shown by the labor-demand or MRP curve because firms demand labor only for the revenue it helps create. That position matters because it It links final-product demand to input demand.
vocabulary.used_for: Use Derived Demand to label or explain the curve on AP Micro graphs, then connect that visual to price, quantity, welfare, or efficiency.
vocabulary.question_types: definition, graph interpretation, multiple-choice reasoning, FRQ explanation, calculation
vocabulary.related_graphs: Competitive Labor Market, Firm Hiring Rule: MRP = MRC
vocabulary.graph_where: Shown by the labor-demand or MRP curve because firms demand labor only for the revenue it helps create.
vocabulary.graph_meaning: It links final-product demand to input demand.
vocabulary.graph_effect: If demand for the final product rises, the labor-demand curve shifts right.
vocabulary.graph_location_text: On the labor-demand or MRP curve, because firms demand labor for the output labor helps produce.
vocabulary.real_example: If restaurants sell more meals because tourism rises, they hire more servers because the demand for labor rises with demand for restaurant output.
vocabulary.example_graph_effect: Higher output demand shifts the labor-demand or MRP curve to the right.
vocabulary.visual_summary: On the labor-demand or MRP curve, because firms demand labor for the output labor helps produce.
vocabulary.related_terms: Labor Demand, Demand for Labor, Marginal Revenue Product, Resource Demand Shifters
vocabulary.confusion: Do not treat labor demand as direct consumer demand; it depends on demand for the final product.
vocabulary.exam_tip: It links final-product demand to input demand.

vocabulary.short_definition: The principle that adding more of a variable input to fixed inputs eventually raises output by smaller and smaller amounts.
vocabulary.long_definition: The principle that adding more of a variable input to fixed inputs eventually raises output by smaller and smaller amounts. This is a main reason marginal cost rises in the short run. On AP graphs it appears as a point located At the point on the production graph where marginal product stops rising and begins to fall.
vocabulary.used_for: Use Diminishing Marginal Returns to label or explain the point on AP Micro graphs, then connect that visual to price, quantity, welfare, or efficiency.
vocabulary.question_types: definition, graph interpretation, multiple-choice reasoning, FRQ explanation, calculation
vocabulary.related_graphs: Total Product and Marginal Product, Short-Run Cost Curves, Production Possibilities Curve
vocabulary.graph_where: At the point on the production graph where marginal product stops rising and begins to fall.
vocabulary.graph_location_text: At the point on the production graph where marginal product stops rising and begins to fall.
vocabulary.real_example: Adding more baristas to a tiny coffee shop eventually helps less because they run into each other and share the same machines.
vocabulary.example_graph_effect: As marginal product starts falling, the marginal cost curve tends to rise.
vocabulary.visual_summary: At the point on the production graph where marginal product stops rising and begins to fall.
vocabulary.confusion: Watch for similar-looking graph labels and AP wording traps.
vocabulary.exam_tip: AP often uses Diminishing Marginal Returns in short explanations, graph labels, or interpretation questions.

vocabulary.short_definition: A strategy that gives a player the best payoff no matter what the other player does.
vocabulary.long_definition: A strategy that gives a player the best payoff no matter what the other player does. Dominant strategies often help identify the Nash equilibrium in AP payoff matrices. On AP graphs it appears as a matrix strategy located The strategy that gives the highest payoff for one player in every row or column comparison. That position matters because it It is the action a player will choose regardless of the rival's decision.
vocabulary.used_for: Use Dominant Strategy to label or explain the matrix strategy on AP Micro graphs, then connect that visual to price, quantity, welfare, or efficiency.
vocabulary.question_types: definition, graph interpretation, multiple-choice reasoning, FRQ explanation, calculation
vocabulary.graph_where: The strategy that gives the highest payoff for one player in every row or column comparison.
vocabulary.graph_meaning: It is the action a player will choose regardless of the rival's decision.
vocabulary.graph_effect: Dominant strategies often lead directly to the Nash equilibrium.
vocabulary.graph_location_text: The strategy that gives the highest payoff for one player in every row or column comparison.
vocabulary.real_example: If cutting price gives a firm a better payoff whether its rival cuts or not, cutting price is its dominant strategy.
vocabulary.example_graph_effect: Dominant strategy is shown in a payoff matrix by the same best response appearing across multiple rival choices.
vocabulary.visual_summary: The strategy that gives the highest payoff for one player in every row or column comparison.
vocabulary.related_terms: Game Theory, Nash Equilibrium, Prisoner's Dilemma
vocabulary.confusion: Do not confuse dominant strategy with the best joint outcome. A dominant strategy is best for one player regardless of the rival's choice.
vocabulary.exam_tip: It is the action a player will choose regardless of the rival's decision.

vocabulary.short_definition: Total revenue minus explicit costs and implicit opportunity costs.
vocabulary.long_definition: Total revenue minus explicit costs and implicit opportunity costs. A firm can have positive accounting profit but zero economic profit if opportunity costs are fully covered. On AP graphs it appears as a region located In the profit rectangle between price and ATC at the profit-maximizing quantity when price is above ATC.
vocabulary.used_for: Use Economic Profit to label or explain the region on AP Micro graphs, then connect that visual to price, quantity, welfare, or efficiency.
vocabulary.question_types: definition, graph interpretation, multiple-choice reasoning, FRQ explanation, calculation
vocabulary.related_graphs: Perfect Competition Firm, Perfect Competition Market
vocabulary.graph_where: In the profit rectangle between price and ATC at the profit-maximizing quantity when price is above ATC.
vocabulary.graph_location_text: In the profit rectangle between price and ATC at the profit-maximizing quantity when price is above ATC.
vocabulary.real_example: Commodity markets such as wheat are the standard AP setting for economic profit.
vocabulary.example_graph_effect: The graph effect is usually a shaded triangle or rectangle used to measure gains, losses, or deadweight loss.
vocabulary.visual_summary: In the profit rectangle between price and ATC at the profit-maximizing quantity when price is above ATC.
vocabulary.related_formulas: Marginal Revenue Basics, Total Cost, Economic Profit, Average Cost Family, Marginal Cost
vocabulary.confusion: Accounting profit ignores implicit costs, but economic profit includes them.
vocabulary.exam_tip: AP often uses Economic Profit in short explanations, graph labels, or interpretation questions.

vocabulary.short_definition: The way a society organizes production, distribution, and consumption decisions.
vocabulary.long_definition: The way a society organizes production, distribution, and consumption decisions. AP Micro focuses on how incentives and prices allocate scarce resources in different systems. A concrete way to remember it is this: A society must decide whether prices, government plans, or some combination will decide what gets produced. In graph terms, Economic systems are not usually shown with one AP graph, but they determine how resources are allocated and how incentives operate.
vocabulary.used_for: Use Economic System in economic systems questions to identify the concept, explain cause and effect, or justify an AP Micro graph answer.
vocabulary.question_types: definition, graph interpretation, multiple-choice reasoning, FRQ explanation
vocabulary.real_example: A society must decide whether prices, government plans, or some combination will decide what gets produced.
vocabulary.example_graph_effect: Economic systems are not usually shown with one AP graph, but they determine how resources are allocated and how incentives operate.
vocabulary.visual_summary: Think of three columns comparing market, command, and mixed systems rather than one curve.
vocabulary.related_terms: Market Economy, Command Economy, Mixed Economy, Incentives
vocabulary.confusion: Do not treat market, command, and mixed economies as all-or-nothing labels in the real world.
vocabulary.exam_tip: AP often uses Economic System in short explanations, graph labels, or interpretation questions.

vocabulary.short_definition: A PPC point on the frontier that uses all available resources and technology productively.
vocabulary.long_definition: A PPC point on the frontier that uses all available resources and technology productively. Efficient production means you cannot get more of one good without giving up some of the other. On AP graphs it appears as a point located Any point on the PPC frontier. That position matters because it The economy is using all resources productively at that output mix.
vocabulary.used_for: Use Efficient to label or explain the point on AP Micro graphs, then connect that visual to price, quantity, welfare, or efficiency.
vocabulary.question_types: definition, graph interpretation, multiple-choice reasoning, FRQ explanation
vocabulary.graph_where: Any point on the PPC frontier.
vocabulary.graph_meaning: The economy is using all resources productively at that output mix.
vocabulary.graph_effect: Moving to another efficient point changes the mix produced but remains productively efficient.
vocabulary.graph_location_text: At any point on the PPC frontier.
vocabulary.real_example: If all workers and machines are fully used, the economy may operate on the PPC frontier instead of inside it.
vocabulary.example_graph_effect: Efficient points lie directly on the PPC.
vocabulary.visual_summary: At any point on the PPC frontier.
vocabulary.confusion: Efficient on a PPC means on the frontier, not just producing a lot.
vocabulary.exam_tip: The economy is using all resources productively at that output mix.

vocabulary.short_definition: The factor of production that organizes resources, takes risk, and starts productive activity.
vocabulary.long_definition: The factor of production that organizes resources, takes risk, and starts productive activity. Entrepreneurs respond to incentives and profit opportunities when deciding what to produce. A concrete way to remember it is this: A standard AP Micro scenario can use entrepreneurship to explain decision-making, incentives, or market outcomes. In graph terms, The graph effect is usually to change which curve shifts, which point matters, or whether quantity is above or below the efficient level.
vocabulary.used_for: Use Entrepreneurship in economic systems questions to identify the concept, explain cause and effect, or justify an AP Micro graph answer.
vocabulary.question_types: definition, graph interpretation, multiple-choice reasoning, FRQ explanation
vocabulary.real_example: A standard AP Micro scenario can use entrepreneurship to explain decision-making, incentives, or market outcomes.
vocabulary.example_graph_effect: The graph effect is usually to change which curve shifts, which point matters, or whether quantity is above or below the efficient level.
vocabulary.visual_summary: The graph effect is usually to change which curve shifts, which point matters, or whether quantity is above or below the efficient level.
vocabulary.confusion: Watch for similar-looking graph labels and AP wording traps.
vocabulary.exam_tip: AP often uses Entrepreneurship in short explanations, graph labels, or interpretation questions.

vocabulary.short_definition: The market-clearing price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
vocabulary.long_definition: The market-clearing price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. On a graph, read equilibrium price off the vertical axis from the supply-demand intersection. On AP graphs it appears as a axis label located On the vertical axis at the price read from the demand-supply intersection.
vocabulary.used_for: Use Equilibrium Price to label or explain the axis label on AP Micro graphs, then connect that visual to price, quantity, welfare, or efficiency.
vocabulary.question_types: definition, graph interpretation, multiple-choice reasoning, FRQ explanation, calculation
vocabulary.related_graphs: Supply and Demand Equilibrium, Consumer and Producer Surplus, Competitive Labor Market
vocabulary.graph_where: On the vertical axis at the price read from the demand-supply intersection.
vocabulary.graph_location_text: On the vertical axis at the price read from the demand-supply intersection.
vocabulary.real_example: A market for tickets, coffee, or gas can use equilibrium price to explain who gains from trade and why equilibrium matters.
vocabulary.example_graph_effect: On the graph, it changes how you interpret the equilibrium point and the welfare areas around it.
vocabulary.visual_summary: On the vertical axis at the price read from the demand-supply intersection.
vocabulary.confusion: Watch for similar-looking graph labels and AP wording traps.
vocabulary.exam_tip: AP often uses Equilibrium Price in short explanations, graph labels, or interpretation questions.

vocabulary.short_definition: The market-clearing quantity at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
vocabulary.long_definition: The market-clearing quantity at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. On a graph, read equilibrium quantity off the horizontal axis from the supply-demand intersection. On AP graphs it appears as a axis label located On the horizontal axis at the quantity read from the demand-supply intersection.
vocabulary.used_for: Use Equilibrium Quantity to label or explain the axis label on AP Micro graphs, then connect that visual to price, quantity, welfare, or efficiency.
vocabulary.question_types: definition, graph interpretation, multiple-choice reasoning, FRQ explanation, calculation
vocabulary.related_graphs: Supply and Demand Equilibrium, Consumer and Producer Surplus
vocabulary.graph_where: On the horizontal axis at the quantity read from the demand-supply intersection.
vocabulary.graph_location_text: On the horizontal axis at the quantity read from the demand-supply intersection.
vocabulary.real_example: A market for tickets, coffee, or gas can use equilibrium quantity to explain who gains from trade and why equilibrium matters.
vocabulary.example_graph_effect: On the graph, it changes how you interpret the equilibrium point and the welfare areas around it.
vocabulary.visual_summary: On the horizontal axis at the quantity read from the demand-supply intersection.
vocabulary.confusion: Watch for similar-looking graph labels and AP wording traps.
vocabulary.exam_tip: AP often uses Equilibrium Quantity in short explanations, graph labels, or interpretation questions.

vocabulary.short_definition: The market-clearing amount of labor hired where labor demand equals labor supply.
vocabulary.long_definition: The market-clearing amount of labor hired where labor demand equals labor supply. On the graph, it is read on the horizontal axis at the labor-market intersection. On AP graphs it appears as a point located On the horizontal axis read from the labor-market intersection. That position matters because it It is the amount of labor hired at equilibrium.
vocabulary.used_for: Use Equilibrium Quantity of Labor to label or explain the point on AP Micro graphs, then connect that visual to price, quantity, welfare, or efficiency.
vocabulary.question_types: definition, graph interpretation, multiple-choice reasoning, FRQ explanation, calculation
vocabulary.graph_where: On the horizontal axis read from the labor-market intersection.
vocabulary.graph_meaning: It is the amount of labor hired at equilibrium.
vocabulary.graph_effect: It rises when labor demand or labor supply shifts right.
vocabulary.graph_location_text: On the horizontal axis at the employment level read from the labor-market intersection.
vocabulary.real_example: If the labor-market intersection occurs at 800 workers, that is the equilibrium quantity of labor.
vocabulary.example_graph_effect: Any shift in labor demand or labor supply changes the equilibrium quantity hired.
vocabulary.visual_summary: On the horizontal axis at the employment level read from the labor-market intersection.
vocabulary.related_terms: Equilibrium Wage, Labor Market Equilibrium, Competitive Labor Market
vocabulary.confusion: Watch for similar-looking graph labels and AP wording traps.
vocabulary.exam_tip: It is the amount of labor hired at equilibrium.

vocabulary.short_definition: The market-clearing wage where the quantity of labor demanded equals the quantity of labor supplied.
vocabulary.long_definition: The market-clearing wage where the quantity of labor demanded equals the quantity of labor supplied. On the graph, it is read on the vertical axis at the labor-market intersection. On AP graphs it appears as a point located On the vertical axis read from the labor-market intersection. That position matters because it It is the wage that clears the labor market.
vocabulary.used_for: Use Equilibrium Wage to label or explain the point on AP Micro graphs, then connect that visual to price, quantity, welfare, or efficiency.
vocabulary.question_types: definition, graph interpretation, multiple-choice reasoning, FRQ explanation, calculation
vocabulary.graph_where: On the vertical axis read from the labor-market intersection.
vocabulary.graph_meaning: It is the wage that clears the labor market.
vocabulary.graph_effect: It rises when labor demand increases or labor supply decreases.
vocabulary.graph_location_text: On the vertical axis at the wage read from the labor-market intersection.
vocabulary.real_example: If labor demand and labor supply intersect at $24 per hour, that is the equilibrium wage.
vocabulary.example_graph_effect: A rightward labor-demand shift raises the equilibrium wage if labor supply does not shift too.
vocabulary.visual_summary: On the vertical axis at the wage read from the labor-market intersection.
vocabulary.related_terms: Equilibrium Quantity of Labor, Labor Market Equilibrium, Competitive Labor Market
vocabulary.confusion: Do not confuse the wage paid by a monopsonist with the competitive equilibrium wage.
vocabulary.exam_tip: It is the wage that clears the labor market.

vocabulary.short_definition: The gap between a firm's actual output and the output at minimum average total cost.
vocabulary.long_definition: The gap between a firm's actual output and the output at minimum average total cost. Monopolistically competitive firms keep excess capacity in long-run equilibrium because they face downward-sloping demand. On AP graphs it appears as a shaded region / gap located The gap between the firm's chosen output and the output at minimum ATC on the long-run graph. That position matters because it It shows that the firm is not producing at the lowest average total cost.
vocabulary.used_for: Use Excess Capacity to label or explain the shaded region / gap on AP Micro graphs, then connect that visual to price, quantity, welfare, or efficiency.
vocabulary.question_types: definition, graph interpretation, multiple-choice reasoning, FRQ explanation, calculation
vocabulary.graph_where: The gap between the firm's chosen output and the output at minimum ATC on the long-run graph.
vocabulary.graph_meaning: It shows that the firm is not producing at the lowest average total cost.
vocabulary.graph_effect: Greater product differentiation and downward-sloping demand can leave the firm farther from minimum ATC.
vocabulary.graph_location_text: In the gap between the firm's chosen output and the lower output that would minimize ATC.
vocabulary.real_example: A cafe in monopolistic competition may operate with empty tables in the long run because it does not produce at minimum ATC.
vocabulary.example_graph_effect: On the long-run monopolistic-competition graph, the firm's output is left of the minimum-ATC quantity.
vocabulary.visual_summary: In the gap between the firm's chosen output and the lower output that would minimize ATC.
vocabulary.related_formulas: Marginal Revenue Basics, Economic Profit, Imperfect Competition Profit Rule, Efficiency in Imperfect Competition
vocabulary.related_terms: Monopolistic Competition, Productive Inefficiency, Average Total Cost
vocabulary.confusion: Excess capacity is not unused factory space in the ordinary sense; on AP graphs it is the gap from minimum ATC output.
vocabulary.exam_tip: It shows that the firm is not producing at the lowest average total cost.

vocabulary.short_definition: A cost or benefit from a market activity that falls on a third party not directly involved in the transaction.
vocabulary.long_definition: A cost or benefit from a market activity that falls on a third party not directly involved in the transaction. Externalities can be positive or negative and can come from production or consumption, which is why Unit 6 compares private and social curves. On AP graphs it appears as a full graph pattern located On an externality graph, in the gap between private and social curves that separates the market quantity from the socially efficient quantity.
vocabulary.used_for: Use Externality to label or explain the full graph pattern on AP Micro graphs, then connect that visual to price, quantity, welfare, or efficiency.
vocabulary.question_types: definition, graph interpretation, multiple-choice reasoning, FRQ explanation, calculation
vocabulary.graph_where: On an externality graph, in the gap between private and social curves that separates the market quantity from the socially efficient quantity.
vocabulary.graph_location_text: On an externality graph, in the gap between private and social curves that separates the market quantity from the socially efficient quantity.
vocabulary.real_example: Factory pollution harms nearby residents even though they are not part of the factory's transactions.
vocabulary.example_graph_effect: Negative externalities push social cost above private cost, while positive externalities push social benefit above private benefit.
vocabulary.visual_summary: On an externality graph, in the gap between private and social curves that separates the market quantity from the socially efficient quantity.
vocabulary.related_terms: Negative Externality, Positive Externality, Social Cost, Social Benefit, Socially Optimal Quantity
vocabulary.confusion: Watch for similar-looking graph labels and AP wording traps.
vocabulary.exam_tip: AP often uses Externality in short explanations, graph labels, or interpretation questions.

vocabulary.short_definition: A market in which firms buy productive resources such as labor, land, or capital.
vocabulary.long_definition: A market in which firms buy productive resources such as labor, land, or capital. AP Micro Unit 5 focuses mostly on labor as the factor of production being bought. A concrete way to remember it is this: A local labor market where hospitals hire nurses is a factor market because firms are buying labor services. In graph terms, The factor-market graph shows firms on the demand side and workers on the supply side instead of buyers and sellers of final goods.
vocabulary.used_for: Use Factor Market in factor markets questions to identify the concept, explain cause and effect, or justify an AP Micro graph answer.
vocabulary.question_types: definition, graph interpretation, multiple-choice reasoning, FRQ explanation, calculation
vocabulary.related_graphs: Competitive Labor Market, Firm Hiring Rule: MRP = MRC, Monopsony
vocabulary.real_example: A local labor market where hospitals hire nurses is a factor market because firms are buying labor services.
vocabulary.example_graph_effect: The factor-market graph shows firms on the demand side and workers on the supply side instead of buyers and sellers of final goods.
vocabulary.visual_summary: Swap the product-market idea of demand and supply into a labor setting with wages on the vertical axis.
vocabulary.related_formulas: Marginal Revenue Product, Hiring Rule for Labor
vocabulary.related_terms: Resource Market, Labor Demand, Labor Supply, Monopsony
vocabulary.confusion: Watch for similar-looking graph labels and AP wording traps.
vocabulary.exam_tip: AP often uses Factor Market in short explanations, graph labels, or interpretation questions.

vocabulary.short_definition: The productive resources used to make goods and services: land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship.
vocabulary.long_definition: The productive resources used to make goods and services: land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship. These inputs become the subject of Unit 5 factor-market analysis later in the course. A concrete way to remember it is this: A standard AP Micro scenario can use factors of production to explain decision-making, incentives, or market outcomes. In graph terms, The graph effect is usually to change which curve shifts, which point matters, or whether quantity is above or below the efficient level.
vocabulary.used_for: Use Factors of Production in economic systems questions to identify the concept, explain cause and effect, or justify an AP Micro graph answer.
vocabulary.question_types: definition, graph interpretation, multiple-choice reasoning, FRQ explanation
vocabulary.real_example: A standard AP Micro scenario can use factors of production to explain decision-making, incentives, or market outcomes.
vocabulary.example_graph_effect: The graph effect is usually to change which curve shifts, which point matters, or whether quantity is above or below the efficient level.
vocabulary.visual_summary: The graph effect is usually to change which curve shifts, which point matters, or whether quantity is above or below the efficient level.
vocabulary.confusion: Watch for similar-looking graph labels and AP wording traps.
vocabulary.exam_tip: AP often uses Factors of Production in short explanations, graph labels, or interpretation questions.

vocabulary.short_definition: A person who receives the benefit of a good without paying for it.
vocabulary.long_definition: A person who receives the benefit of a good without paying for it. Free riders are the reason a privately supplied public good may not collect enough revenue to cover its cost. On AP graphs it appears as a behavior cue located In the public-good panel next to the unpaid-benefit example. That position matters because it It identifies a person who benefits without paying.
vocabulary.used_for: Use Free Rider to label or explain the behavior cue on AP Micro graphs, then connect that visual to price, quantity, welfare, or efficiency.
vocabulary.question_types: definition, graph interpretation, multiple-choice reasoning, FRQ explanation
vocabulary.graph_where: In the public-good panel next to the unpaid-benefit example.
vocabulary.graph_meaning: It identifies a person who benefits without paying.
vocabulary.graph_effect: As free riding rises, private incentives to provide the good weaken.
vocabulary.graph_location_text: In the left public-good panel as the example of a nonpayer still receiving the benefit.
vocabulary.real_example: A resident who enjoys neighborhood street lighting without helping pay the tax bill is a free rider.
vocabulary.example_graph_effect: Each free rider weakens the private incentive to supply a public good because the seller cannot easily collect payment from everyone who benefits.
vocabulary.visual_summary: In the left public-good panel as the example of a nonpayer still receiving the benefit.
vocabulary.confusion: A free rider is a person; the free-rider problem is the broader market failure that follows.
vocabulary.exam_tip: It identifies a person who benefits without paying.

vocabulary.short_definition: A market failure in which people can benefit from a good without paying, causing underprovision.
vocabulary.long_definition: A market failure in which people can benefit from a good without paying, causing underprovision. Street lighting is a simple example: many people benefit even if some do not contribute, so private sellers struggle to collect enough revenue. On AP graphs it appears as a behavior cue located In the public-good panel where private demand is weaker than total social benefit. That position matters because it It explains why public goods are often underprovided in ordinary private markets.
vocabulary.used_for: Use Free Rider Problem to label or explain the behavior cue on AP Micro graphs, then connect that visual to price, quantity, welfare, or efficiency.
vocabulary.question_types: definition, graph interpretation, multiple-choice reasoning, FRQ explanation
vocabulary.graph_where: In the public-good panel where private demand is weaker than total social benefit.
vocabulary.graph_meaning: It explains why public goods are often underprovided in ordinary private markets.
vocabulary.graph_effect: Government taxation or public provision can move supply closer to the socially desirable amount.
vocabulary.graph_location_text: In the left public-good panel where private willingness to pay understates full social benefit.
vocabulary.real_example: A resident may enjoy fireworks or national defense even if they refuse to help pay for them.
vocabulary.example_graph_effect: The problem helps explain why market demand for public goods is understated and why private markets underprovide them.
vocabulary.visual_summary: In the left public-good panel where private willingness to pay understates full social benefit.
vocabulary.related_terms: Free Rider, Public Good, Social Benefit
vocabulary.confusion: Watch for similar-looking graph labels and AP wording traps.
vocabulary.exam_tip: It explains why public goods are often underprovided in ordinary private markets.

vocabulary.short_definition: The increase in total output or consumption possibilities that occurs when producers specialize and trade according to comparative advantage.
vocabulary.long_definition: The increase in total output or consumption possibilities that occurs when producers specialize and trade according to comparative advantage. Both sides can gain even when one side has absolute advantage in everything. On AP graphs it appears as a outcome note located In the trade outcome section comparing before-trade and after-trade consumption possibilities. That position matters because it It shows why both sides can consume beyond their no-trade alternatives.
vocabulary.used_for: Use Gains from Trade to label or explain the outcome note on AP Micro graphs, then connect that visual to price, quantity, welfare, or efficiency.
vocabulary.question_types: definition, graph interpretation, multiple-choice reasoning, FRQ explanation
vocabulary.related_graphs: Comparative Advantage and Trade Table, Production Possibilities Curve
vocabulary.graph_where: In the trade outcome section comparing before-trade and after-trade consumption possibilities.
vocabulary.graph_meaning: It shows why both sides can consume beyond their no-trade alternatives.
vocabulary.graph_effect: As long as terms of trade fall between opportunity costs, both sides can gain.
vocabulary.graph_location_text: In the after-trade outcome line showing both sides can consume beyond their no-trade options.
vocabulary.real_example: If two students trade notes or labor tasks based on comparative advantage, both can end up better off than if each worked alone.
vocabulary.example_graph_effect: Trade can move consumption beyond a producer's own PPC because specialization expands what is available to exchange.
vocabulary.visual_summary: In the after-trade outcome line showing both sides can consume beyond their no-trade options.
vocabulary.related_terms: Comparative Advantage, Specialization, Terms of Trade
vocabulary.confusion: Trade gains come from comparative advantage and terms of trade, not simply from one side producing more of everything.
vocabulary.exam_tip: It shows why both sides can consume beyond their no-trade alternatives.

vocabulary.short_definition: The study of strategic decision-making when each player's payoff depends on the choices of others.
vocabulary.long_definition: The study of strategic decision-making when each player's payoff depends on the choices of others. AP Micro uses game theory mainly to analyze oligopoly behavior and collusion problems. On AP graphs it appears as a matrix located Inside a 2x2 payoff matrix comparing each firm's strategic options. That position matters because it It shows how each player's payoff depends on the rival's choice.
vocabulary.used_for: Use Game Theory to label or explain the matrix on AP Micro graphs, then connect that visual to price, quantity, welfare, or efficiency.
vocabulary.question_types: definition, graph interpretation, multiple-choice reasoning, FRQ explanation, calculation
vocabulary.graph_where: Inside a 2x2 payoff matrix comparing each firm's strategic options.
vocabulary.graph_meaning: It shows how each player's payoff depends on the rival's choice.
vocabulary.graph_effect: Best responses determine dominant strategies and Nash equilibrium.
vocabulary.graph_location_text: Inside a 2x2 payoff matrix comparing each firm's strategic options.
vocabulary.real_example: Two airlines deciding whether to keep fares high or cut them must think about how the rival will react.
vocabulary.example_graph_effect: Game theory is usually visualized with a payoff matrix rather than a standard supply-and-demand graph.
vocabulary.visual_summary: Inside a 2x2 payoff matrix comparing each firm's strategic options.
vocabulary.related_terms: Dominant Strategy, Nash Equilibrium, Prisoner's Dilemma, Oligopoly

vocabulary.short_definition: An economic system in which households and firms make most decisions through voluntary exchange and price signals.
vocabulary.long_definition: An economic system in which households and firms make most decisions through voluntary exchange and price signals. Private property and incentives play a major role in resource allocation. A concrete way to remember it is this: In a market economy, higher demand for electric cars tends to raise production because prices and profit signals guide firms. In graph terms, Price signals in markets help move resources toward goods with higher demand and profit opportunities.

vocabulary.long_definition: A formula that uses average starting and ending values to calculate percentage changes consistently. vocabulary.short_definition: An economy that combines market forces with government intervention and regulation.
vocabulary.long_definition: An economy that combines market forces with government intervention and regulation. Most modern economies are mixed rather than purely market or purely command systems. A concrete way to remember it is this: The United States uses markets for many decisions but also has taxes, public schools, regulations, and transfer programs. In graph terms, Mixed economies use markets as a base while government policies reshape incentives and outcomes.

vocabulary.short_definition: A market structure with a single seller that faces no close substitutes and strong barriers to entry.
vocabulary.long_definition: A market structure with a single seller that faces no close substitutes and strong barriers to entry. A monopolist is a price maker and chooses output where MR = MC, then reads price from demand. A concrete way to remember it is this: A local water utility or electric provider is a classic monopoly example because one firm serves the market and entry is difficult. In graph terms, The monopolist restricts output where MR = MC and charges the price on the demand curve at that quantity.

vocabulary.long_definition: Marginal private benefit, or the benefit received by the direct buyer or user of the good. MPB is the private-market benefit curve; if there is a positive externality, it lies below MSB. On AP graphs it appears as a curve located The lower downward-sloping private-benefit curve below MSB. That position matters because it It shows the direct buyer's or user's benefit from one more unit.

vocabulary.long_definition: Marginal private cost, or the cost borne by producers or consumers directly involved in the transaction. MPC is the private-market cost curve; if there is a negative externality, it lies below MSC. On AP graphs it appears as a curve located The lower upward-sloping private-cost curve below MSC. vocabulary.short_definition: Marginal social benefit, or the full benefit of one more unit including both private and external benefits.
vocabulary.long_definition: Marginal social benefit, or the full benefit of one more unit including both private and external benefits. With a positive externality, MSB lies above MPB because society gains more than the direct consumer accounts for. On AP graphs it appears as a curve located The higher downward-sloping social-benefit curve above MPB. That position matters because it It includes private benefit plus external benefit to third parties.
vocabulary.used_for: Use MSB to label or explain the curve on AP Micro graphs, then connect that visual to price, quantity, welfare, or efficiency.

vocabulary.long_definition: Marginal social cost, or the full cost of one more unit including both private cost and external cost. vocabulary.example_graph_effect: On a negative externality graph, MSC is the upper cost curve above MPC and it determines the socially optimal quantity with MSB.

vocabulary.long_definition: An outcome in which each player's strategy is optimal given the strategies of others. In AP Micro, oligopoly game theory questions often compare individual incentive with joint outcome. vocabulary.short_definition: A monopoly that exists because one firm can supply the market at a lower average total cost than multiple competing firms.
vocabulary.long_definition: A monopoly that exists because one firm can supply the market at a lower average total cost than multiple competing firms. This often happens when fixed costs are very large, such as with utilities or water systems. vocabulary.short_definition: A situation in which a firm does not produce at the lowest possible average total cost.
vocabulary.long_definition: A situation in which a firm does not produce at the lowest possible average total cost. vocabulary.long_definition: The condition that arises because human wants are unlimited while resources are limited. Scarcity is the reason economics studies choice and tradeoffs. A concrete way to remember it is this: A city has limited land, labor, and capital, so it cannot build every road, school, and hospital citizens want at the same time. In graph terms, Scarcity is why the PPC exists at all: the frontier marks the limit created by finite resources.

vocabulary.long_definition: In the short run, a competitive firm should keep producing if price is at least average variable cost. If price falls below AVC, shutting down minimizes losses. A concrete way to remember it is this: A bakery may stay open in the short run even with losses if daily sales still cover flour, labor, and utilities. In graph terms, If price stays above AVC, the firm keeps producing; if price falls below AVC, it shuts down in the short run.

graphs.title: Supply and Demand Equilibrium
graphs.overview_page:
Used for
Use this as the base graph before adding taxes, subsidies, shortages, surpluses, or welfare areas.

Axes
Y-axis: Price | X-axis: Quantity

Curves
Downward-sloping demand, upward-sloping supply, equilibrium at their intersection

Equilibrium / key outcome
Demand right raises equilibrium price and quantity. Supply right lowers price and raises quantity.
graphs.labels_page:
Curve labels
Downward-sloping demand, upward-sloping supply, equilibrium at their intersection

Point and area cues
Equilibrium is where Qd = Qs and total surplus is maximized.
graphs.shifts_page:
Shifts / causes
Demand shifts from income, tastes, expectations, population, prices of related goods. Supply shifts from input costs, technology, taxes/subsidies, seller count, expectations.

What changes
Demand right raises equilibrium price and quantity. Supply right lowers price and raises quantity.

What does not shift
Price alone does not shift the curve being measured; watch for determinant changes instead.

Movement along curves
A change in the graph's own axis variable moves you along the existing curve.
graphs.guide_page:
Reading guide

1. Find the intersection. 2. Read equilibrium price and quantity. 3. Decide whether a curve shifted or price changed on an existing curve. 4. Check how price and quantity changed.
graphs.questions_page:
Common AP questions

Identify equilibrium price and quantity. Explain the effect of a demand or supply shift. Distinguish movement along a curve from a shift.
graphs.mistakes_page:
Common mistakes

Do not say price changes shift demand or supply. Price changes move along the existing curve.

graphs.title: Production Possibilities Curve
graphs.topic_ids_csv: scarcity-choice, opportunity-cost, ppc, comparative-advantage, specialization-trade, production-functions
graphs.overview_page:
Used for
PPC questions are about tradeoffs, efficiency, growth, and opportunity cost.

Axes
Y-axis: Good B | X-axis: Good A

Curves
A bowed-out frontier for increasing opportunity cost or a straight line for constant opportunity cost

Equilibrium / key outcome
Points on the curve are efficient, inside are inefficient, outside are unattainable with current resources.
graphs.labels_page:
Curve labels
A bowed-out frontier for increasing opportunity cost or a straight line for constant opportunity cost

Point and area cues
Moving along the PPC changes the mix produced; shifting the PPC changes productive capacity.
graphs.shifts_page:
Shifts / causes
Outward shift from growth, more resources, or better technology. Inward shift from disasters or resource loss.

What changes
Points on the curve are efficient, inside are inefficient, outside are unattainable with current resources.

What does not shift
Price alone does not shift the curve being measured; watch for determinant changes instead.

Movement along curves
A change in the graph's own axis variable moves you along the existing curve.
graphs.guide_page:
Reading guide

1. Identify the frontier. 2. Classify a point as on the curve, inside it, or outside it. 3. Use movement along the frontier to explain opportunity cost. 4. Use a shifted frontier to explain growth or productivity change.
graphs.questions_page:
Common AP questions

Is the point efficient, inefficient, or unattainable? What is the opportunity cost of moving along the frontier? What causes the PPC to shift outward?
graphs.mistakes_page:
Common mistakes

Do not call a point inside the PPC unattainable. Do not forget that movement along the frontier is different from shifting the whole frontier.

graphs.title: Comparative Advantage and Trade Table
graphs.overview_page:
Used for
Use this visual when trade logic is clearer in a table than on a PPC. It is especially useful for absolute advantage, comparative advantage, specialization, and gains from trade.

Axes
Rows: producers | Columns: outputs and opportunity costs

Curves
No curves; this is a compact production and opportunity-cost comparison table

Equilibrium / key outcome
Lower opportunity cost determines comparative advantage and therefore specialization. Gains from trade appear when trade terms fall between the two opportunity costs.
graphs.labels_page:
Curve labels
No curves; this is a compact production and opportunity-cost comparison table

Point and area cues
Absolute advantage is about more output. Comparative advantage is about lower opportunity cost.
graphs.shifts_page:
Shifts / causes
This visual is about comparing opportunity costs and specialization choices rather than curve shifts.

What changes
Lower opportunity cost determines comparative advantage and therefore specialization. Gains from trade appear when trade terms fall between the two opportunity costs.

What does not shift
Price alone does not shift the curve being measured; watch for determinant changes instead.

Movement along curves
A change in the graph's own axis variable moves you along the existing curve.
graphs.guide_page:
Reading guide

1. Compare total output first for absolute advantage. 2. Compare opportunity costs for comparative advantage. 3. Match each producer to the lower-opportunity-cost good. 4. Check whether the terms of trade fall between the two opportunity costs.
graphs.questions_page:
Common AP questions

Who has absolute advantage? Who has comparative advantage? Who should specialize in each good? Are there gains from trade?
graphs.mistakes_page:
Common mistakes

Do not use absolute advantage to decide specialization. Comparative advantage depends on lower opportunity cost.

graphs.title: Per-Unit Tax
graphs.overview_page:
Used for
The less elastic side of the market bears more of the tax burden.

Axes
Y-axis: Price | X-axis: Quantity

Curves
Original supply, demand, and taxed supply shifted upward by the tax amount

Equilibrium / key outcome
Quantity falls, buyer price rises, seller price falls, government collects a rectangle, and DWL appears.
graphs.labels_page:
Curve labels
Original supply, demand, and taxed supply shifted upward by the tax amount

Point and area cues
Tax revenue uses post-tax quantity. DWL is the triangle formed by lost trades.
graphs.shifts_page:
Shifts / causes
A per-unit tax creates a vertical wedge between buyer price and seller price.

What changes
Quantity falls, buyer price rises, seller price falls, government collects a rectangle, and DWL appears.

What does not shift
Price alone does not shift the curve being measured; watch for determinant changes instead.

Movement along curves
A change in the graph's own axis variable moves you along the existing curve.
graphs.guide_page:
Reading guide

1. Find the original equilibrium. 2. Shift supply up by the tax. 3. Read buyer price, seller price, and new quantity. 4. Rectangle is tax revenue. Triangle is deadweight loss.
graphs.questions_page:
Common AP questions

Who bears more of the tax? What is tax revenue? What is deadweight loss? How does quantity change?
graphs.mistakes_page:
Common mistakes

Do not use pre-tax quantity for tax revenue. Do not assume the legal payer bears the full burden.

graphs.title: Per-Unit Subsidy
graphs.overview_page:
Used for
This graph is the mirror image of a tax graph.

Axes
Y-axis: Price | X-axis: Quantity

Curves
Original supply, demand, and subsidized supply shifted downward by the subsidy amount

Equilibrium / key outcome
Quantity rises beyond the efficient level, government spending is a rectangle, and overproduction creates DWL.
graphs.labels_page:
Curve labels
Original supply, demand, and subsidized supply shifted downward by the subsidy amount

Point and area cues
The DWL triangle sits to the right of the original equilibrium quantity.
graphs.shifts_page:
Shifts / causes
A per-unit subsidy creates a wedge between the price paid by buyers and the price received by sellers.

What changes
Quantity rises beyond the efficient level, government spending is a rectangle, and overproduction creates DWL.

What does not shift
Price alone does not shift the curve being measured; watch for determinant changes instead.

Movement along curves
A change in the graph's own axis variable moves you along the existing curve.
graphs.guide_page:
Reading guide

1. Find the original equilibrium. 2. Shift supply down by the subsidy. 3. Read buyer price, seller price, and new quantity. 4. Rectangle is government spending. Triangle is overproduction DWL.
graphs.questions_page:
Common AP questions

What is government spending? Where is deadweight loss? Why is output above the efficient level?
graphs.mistakes_page:
Common mistakes

Do not place the DWL triangle on the left side of equilibrium. Subsidies create overproduction to the right.

Used for
Use this for rent control or anti-price-gouging style questions.

Axes
Y-axis: Price | X-axis: Quantity

Curves
Demand and supply with a horizontal price line below equilibrium

Equilibrium / key outcome
Quantity demanded rises, quantity supplied falls, and a shortage appears.

Curve labels
Demand and supply with a horizontal price line below equilibrium

Point and area cues
The quantity actually exchanged is limited by the short side of the market, usually quantity supplied.
graphs.shifts_page:
Shifts / causes
No curve shifts; policy fixes price below equilibrium.

What changes
Quantity demanded rises, quantity supplied falls, and a shortage appears.

What does not shift
Price alone does not shift the curve being measured; watch for determinant changes instead.

Movement along curves
A change in the graph's own axis variable moves you along the existing curve.
graphs.guide_page:
Reading guide

1. Compare the ceiling to equilibrium price. 2. If it is below equilibrium, it binds. 3. Read quantity supplied and quantity demanded at the ceiling. 4. The gap is shortage.
graphs.questions_page:
Common AP questions

Is the ceiling binding? What shortage is created? What quantity is actually exchanged?
graphs.mistakes_page:
Common mistakes

Do not confuse shortage with surplus. A low binding price ceiling causes shortage.

graphs.title: Monopolistic Competition

Used for

Equilibrium / key outcome
In the long run, firms earn zero economic profit but still do not produce at minimum ATC, so excess capacity remains.

Curve labels
Downward-sloping demand, MR below demand, MC and ATC

Point and area cues
Long-run equilibrium still leaves excess capacity and productive inefficiency even after economic profit disappears.

Long-run entry shifts a firm's demand left until price equals ATC.

In the long run, firms earn zero economic profit but still do not produce at minimum ATC, so excess capacity remains.

Movement along curves
A change in the graph's own axis variable moves you along the existing curve.

Reading guide

Common AP questions

Find short-run price and quantity, explain long-run zero economic profit, and identify excess capacity.
graphs.mistakes_page:
Common mistakes

Do not call long-run zero economic profit efficient. The firm still has excess capacity and P still exceeds MC.

graphs.title: Oligopoly and Kinked Demand

Used for

Axes

Curves
A kinked demand curve with a broken MR curve below it and MC crossing the MR gap

Equilibrium / key outcome
Firms may keep the same price even when marginal cost changes within the MR gap because rivals are expected to match cuts but not increases.
graphs.labels_page:
Curve labels
A kinked demand curve with a broken MR curve below it and MC crossing the MR gap

Point and area cues
Kinked demand is not the only oligopoly model, but it is a standard AP way to show sticky prices.
graphs.shifts_page:
Shifts / causes
The model emphasizes price rigidity more than clean shifts, but large cost changes can move output if MC leaves the MR gap.

What changes
Firms may keep the same price even when marginal cost changes within the MR gap because rivals are expected to match cuts but not increases.

What does not shift
Price alone does not shift the curve being measured; watch for determinant changes instead.

Movement along curves
A change in the graph's own axis variable moves you along the existing curve.

Reading guide

1. Identify the kink in the demand curve. 2. Notice the broken MR curve beneath it. 3. If MC moves inside the MR gap, price and output may stay sticky.
graphs.questions_page:
Common AP questions

Why might price stay rigid? What happens if MC changes within the MR gap? How does interdependence affect pricing?
graphs.mistakes_page:
Common mistakes

Do not treat the kinked-demand model like an ordinary smooth monopoly graph. The broken MR curve is the point of the model.

No curves; this is a 2x2 payoff matrix showing strategic outcomes

A dominant strategy is best regardless of the rival's move; Nash equilibrium is where neither player wants to move alone.

Shifts / causes
There are no curve shifts here. Instead, compare payoffs to find dominant strategies and Nash equilibrium.

Changing the payoff values can change whether firms collude, cheat, or land in a prisoner's dilemma outcome.

A change in the graph's own axis variable moves you along the existing curve.

Common AP questions

What is each firm's dominant strategy? Where is the Nash equilibrium? Why might the equilibrium be worse than collusion?
graphs.mistakes_page:
Common mistakes

Price alone does not shift the curve being measured; watch for determinant changes instead.

Movement along curves
A change in the graph's own axis variable moves you along the existing curve.

Reading guide

1. Use MRP = MFC for hiring. 2. Move down to labor supply to read wage. 3. Compare with competitive outcome to see lower wage and employment.
graphs.questions_page:
Common AP questions

Identify labels, explain shifts, and connect the graph to AP Micro reasoning.
graphs.mistakes_page:
Common mistakes

Do not read wage from MFC. Read wage from labor supply at the chosen quantity.

Downward-sloping labor demand, upward-sloping labor supply, and equilibrium where the two intersect

Downward-sloping labor demand, upward-sloping labor supply, and equilibrium where the two intersect

Use it to identify equilibrium wage, equilibrium quantity of labor, and how labor-demand or labor-supply shifters change both.

Shifts / causes
Output price or productivity changes shift labor demand. Worker preferences, migration, and labor-force size shift labor supply.

The market intersection sets equilibrium wage and equilibrium quantity of labor. A rightward demand shift usually raises both.

Price alone does not shift the curve being measured; watch for determinant changes instead.

A change in the graph's own axis variable moves you along the existing curve.

Reading guide

Common AP questions

Find the equilibrium wage and quantity of labor. Explain what shifts labor demand or labor supply and how the new equilibrium changes.

Downward-sloping MRP and a horizontal wage = MRC line for a wage-taking firm

The firm hires workers up to the point where MRP equals wage, because wage is the firm's marginal resource cost in a competitive labor market.

Curve labels
Downward-sloping MRP and a horizontal wage = MRC line for a wage-taking firm

Point and area cues
If MRP is above wage, hire more labor. If MRP is below wage, hire less labor.
graphs.shifts_page:
Shifts / causes
Higher output price or productivity shifts MRP right/up. A higher wage shifts the MRC line up.

What changes
The firm hires workers up to the point where MRP equals wage, because wage is the firm's marginal resource cost in a competitive labor market.

What does not shift
Price alone does not shift the curve being measured; watch for determinant changes instead.

Movement along curves
A change in the graph's own axis variable moves you along the existing curve.
graphs.guide_page:
Reading guide

1. Read the downward-sloping MRP curve as the benefit of another worker. 2. Read the wage = MRC line as the hiring cost. 3. Hire where the two meet.
graphs.questions_page:
Common AP questions

Should the firm hire more labor, less labor, or stay at the current level? How does a wage change or productivity change affect hiring?

Curve labels
Demand and supply with equilibrium price and shaded welfare triangles

Point and area cues
Consumer surplus is above price and below demand; producer surplus is below price and above supply.
graphs.shifts_page:
Shifts / causes
Anything shifting demand or supply changes the size of the consumer and producer surplus regions.

What changes
Higher prices usually reduce consumer surplus and can increase producer surplus depending on the cause.

What does not shift
Price alone does not shift the curve being measured; watch for determinant changes instead.

Movement along curves
A change in the graph's own axis variable moves you along the existing curve.

Reading guide

1. Find equilibrium. 2. Shade consumer surplus above price and below demand. 3. Shade producer surplus below price and above supply. 4. Total surplus is both areas together.

Common AP questions
