graphs.title: Negative Externality
graphs.overview_page:
Used for
Use this graph to compare the private-market outcome with the socially efficient outcome and to show how a corrective tax or regulation reduces overproduction.

Axes
Y-axis: Cost/Benefit | X-axis: Quantity

Curves
MPC below MSC and MSB as the benefit curve; the market quantity is where MPC meets MSB and the social optimum is where MSC meets MSB

Equilibrium / key outcome
Market quantity is greater than the socially optimal quantity, deadweight loss appears between Qm and Qsoc, and the external-cost gap explains why the market overproduces.
graphs.labels_page:
Curve labels
MPC below MSC and MSB as the benefit curve; the market quantity is where MPC meets MSB and the social optimum is where MSC meets MSB

Point and area cues
Social optimum is where MSB = MSC. Qm is where MPC meets MSB. The DWL triangle lies between those two quantities.
graphs.shifts_page:
Shifts / causes
The external cost creates a vertical gap between MPC and MSC. A corrective tax or regulation works by pushing private decision-making toward MSC.

What changes
Market quantity is greater than the socially optimal quantity, deadweight loss appears between Qm and Qsoc, and the external-cost gap explains why the market overproduces.

What does not shift
Price alone does not shift the curve being measured; watch for determinant changes instead.

Movement along curves
A change in the graph's own axis variable moves you along the existing curve.
graphs.guide_page:
Reading guide

1. Identify MPC, MSC, and MSB. 2. Find Qm where MPC meets MSB. 3. Find Qsoc where MSC meets MSB. 4. The gap between those quantities is overproduction and creates DWL. 5. Explain how a corrective tax or regulation moves Q toward Qsoc.
graphs.questions_page:
Common AP questions

Compare market quantity with socially optimal quantity. Label MPC, MSC, external cost, and deadweight loss. Identify the corrective tax or regulation.
graphs.mistakes_page:
Common mistakes

Do not use private-market equilibrium as the socially efficient quantity. Negative externalities mean overproduction, not underproduction.

Used for
Use this graph to compare the private-market outcome with the socially efficient outcome and to show how a subsidy raises output toward the social optimum.

Curves
MPB below MSB and MSC as the cost curve; the market quantity is where MPB meets MSC and the social optimum is where MSB meets MSC

Market quantity is below the socially optimal quantity, deadweight loss appears between Qm and Qsoc, and the external-benefit gap explains why the market underproduces.

Curve labels
MPB below MSB and MSC as the cost curve; the market quantity is where MPB meets MSC and the social optimum is where MSB meets MSC

Social optimum is where MSB = MSC. Qm is where MPB meets MSC. Vaccines and education are classic AP examples.
graphs.shifts_page:
Shifts / causes
The external benefit creates a vertical gap between MPB and MSB. A corrective subsidy or public support works by pushing private decision-making toward MSB.

What changes
Market quantity is below the socially optimal quantity, deadweight loss appears between Qm and Qsoc, and the external-benefit gap explains why the market underproduces.

What does not shift
Price alone does not shift the curve being measured; watch for determinant changes instead.

Movement along curves
A change in the graph's own axis variable moves you along the existing curve.
graphs.guide_page:
Reading guide

1. Identify MPB, MSB, and MSC. 2. Find Qm where MPB meets MSC. 3. Find Qsoc where MSB meets MSC. 4. The gap between those quantities is underproduction and creates DWL. 5. Explain how a subsidy moves Q toward Qsoc.
graphs.questions_page:
Common AP questions

Show underproduction, label MPB and MSB, and explain how a subsidy or public support can restore efficiency.

graphs.title: Public Goods and Common Resources

Used for
Use this reference visual when AP asks you to classify a good, explain free riding, compare public goods with common resources, or justify government provision or regulation.

Curves
No formal AP curve is required here; this is a reference visual comparing non-rival/non-excludable underprovision with rival/non-excludable overuse

Public goods tend to be underprovided because of free riders. Common resources tend to be overused because each user ignores the social cost imposed on others.

Curve labels
No formal AP curve is required here; this is a reference visual comparing non-rival/non-excludable underprovision with rival/non-excludable overuse

Point and area cues
Public good = non-rival and non-excludable. Common resource = rival and non-excludable. Government provision helps public goods; rules, permits, or property rights help common resources.
graphs.shifts_page:
Shifts / causes
The key changes are not ordinary curve shifts. Instead, focus on how free riding weakens private provision and how open access encourages overuse.

What changes
Public goods tend to be underprovided because of free riders. Common resources tend to be overused because each user ignores the social cost imposed on others.

What does not shift
Price alone does not shift the curve being measured; watch for determinant changes instead.

Movement along curves
A change in the graph's own axis variable moves you along the existing curve.
graphs.guide_page:
Reading guide

1. Classify the good by rivalry and excludability. 2. If it is non-rival and non-excludable, think public good and free-rider underprovision. 3. If it is rival and non-excludable, think common resource and overuse. 4. Match the policy to the problem: public provision for public goods, regulation or property-right tools for common resources.

Common AP questions

Is the good a public good or a common resource? Why does the free-rider problem cause underprovision? Why does open access create overuse? What policy could improve the outcome?
graphs.mistakes_page:

Do not confuse public goods with common resources. Public goods are non-rival; common resources are rival.

formulas.body:
Formula
PED = % change in quantity demanded / % change in price

Variables
Quantity demanded and price measured with midpoint percentages for AP work

When to use it
Use this in demand supply shifts questions when AP asks you to calculate or interpret a numerical result.

How to interpret it
After calculating, explain what the number means for responsiveness, revenue, cost, profit, or efficiency.

Common trap
Use the absolute value for classification. PED > 1 is elastic, PED < 1 is inelastic.

formulas.title: Price Elasticity of Supply
formulas.formula: PES = % change in quantity supplied / % change in price
formulas.variables: Quantity supplied and price measured with midpoint percentages for AP work
formulas.when_to_use: Use this in demand supply shifts questions when AP asks you to calculate or interpret a numerical result.

If MRP is greater than MRC, the firm should hire more labor. If MRP is less than MRC, the firm should hire less.

concepts.title: Scarcity and Choice
concepts.short_definition: Scarcity means resources are limited, so every person and society must choose among competing wants.
concepts.full_explanation: Scarcity is the starting point of economics. Because land, labor, capital, and time are limited, people, firms, and governments cannot do everything they want at once. That forces choices, and each choice creates a trade-off. AP Micro uses this idea to frame opportunity cost, PPC analysis, specialization, and market decision-making. Scarcity is why prices, incentives, and trade matter in the first place.
concepts.why_it_matters: It is the foundation for the rest of the course because every later model is really about how scarce resources are allocated.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks why societies must choose, why trade-offs exist, or why opportunity cost matters.
concepts.real_world_example: A city cannot spend the same dollar on road repair, schools, and parks at the same time, so policymakers must choose which projects to fund now and which to delay.
concepts.graph_connection: The PPC is the standard visual for scarcity because it shows the limit created by current resources and technology.
concepts.graph_location_text: The bowed or straight frontier between the two output axes.
concepts.related_terms: Scarcity, Trade-Off, Opportunity Cost, Production Possibilities Curve
concepts.quick_recall: Unlimited wants plus limited resources means every choice has a cost.

concepts.title: Opportunity Cost
concepts.short_definition: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up when a decision is made.
concepts.full_explanation: Opportunity cost is narrower than a general trade-off because it focuses on the single best alternative forgone. AP Micro uses it constantly: when reading the slope of a PPC, when deciding comparative advantage, and when judging whether a choice is rational. If the benefit of an action is less than the opportunity cost, the decision is not worthwhile from an economic perspective.
concepts.why_it_matters: It is the key reasoning tool behind comparative advantage, PPC movement, and rational decision-making.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks how much of one good must be sacrificed for another, who has comparative advantage, or what the real cost of a choice is.
concepts.real_world_example: If a student spends an extra hour studying economics instead of working for pay, the opportunity cost is the wages and experience from the forgone work hour.
concepts.graph_connection: On a PPC, moving toward more of one good means giving up some of the other good. The slope of the frontier captures that opportunity cost.
concepts.graph_location_text: Along the PPC frontier as you move toward more of one good and less of the other.
concepts.related_terms: Opportunity Cost, Trade-Off, Production Possibilities Curve, Comparative Advantage
concepts.quick_recall: Ask what the next best alternative was and how much of it had to be given up.

concepts.title: Production Possibilities Curve
concepts.short_definition: A PPC shows the maximum combinations of two goods that can be produced with current resources and technology.
concepts.full_explanation: The PPC is one of the most important Unit 1 tools because it packages scarcity, opportunity cost, efficiency, and growth into one graph. Points on the frontier are efficient, points inside the frontier are inefficient, and points outside the frontier are unattainable with current resources and technology. Moving along the PPC shows trade-offs between the two goods, while shifting the whole PPC outward shows growth from more resources, better technology, or higher productivity.
concepts.why_it_matters: It gives AP Micro a visual language for classifying output points and explaining why trade-offs and growth matter.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks whether a point is efficient, inefficient, or unattainable, or when it asks what happens after growth or improved productivity.
concepts.real_world_example: An economy deciding between consumer goods and capital goods can use a PPC to show how producing more of one limits how much of the other can be produced right now.
concepts.graph_connection: The PPC graph itself is the visual model. Focus on the frontier, the location of points, and whether the whole curve shifts.
concepts.graph_location_text: At any point on the PPC frontier.
concepts.related_terms: Production Possibilities Curve, Efficient, Inefficient, Unattainable, Productivity
concepts.quick_recall: On the curve = efficient, inside = inefficient, outside = unattainable, outward shift = growth.

concepts.title: Comparative Advantage
concepts.short_definition: Comparative advantage means producing a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer.
concepts.full_explanation: Comparative advantage is about what a producer gives up, not just how much it can make. A producer with lower opportunity cost in a good should specialize in that good. This can be true even if another producer has an absolute advantage in both goods. AP Micro trade questions nearly always turn on comparing opportunity costs correctly and then identifying who should specialize in what.
concepts.why_it_matters: It explains the logic behind specialization and why trade can benefit both sides.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks who should specialize, who should export a good, or how to identify gains from trade.
concepts.real_world_example: If one country gives up fewer computers to produce wheat than another country does, it has comparative advantage in wheat and should specialize more in wheat production.
concepts.graph_connection: Comparative advantage is often easier to show with a production table or trade schedule than with one curve, so the app links it to a trade-table visual.
concepts.graph_location_text: In the lower opportunity-cost row or comparison cells of the trade table.
concepts.related_terms: Comparative Advantage, Absolute Advantage, Opportunity Cost, Specialization, Gains from Trade
concepts.quick_recall: Lower opportunity cost wins comparative advantage.

concepts.title: Specialization and Trade
concepts.short_definition: Specialization and trade let producers focus on what they do relatively best and then exchange for the rest.
concepts.full_explanation: When producers specialize according to comparative advantage, total output rises or is allocated more efficiently. Trade then lets both sides consume combinations they could not reach alone. The gains from trade depend on opportunity cost and the terms of trade. If the agreed trade rate falls between the two producers' opportunity costs, both sides benefit.
concepts.why_it_matters: It is the payoff of Unit 1 trade logic: comparative advantage matters because it makes specialization and trade beneficial.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks whether trade is mutually beneficial, whether the terms of trade are acceptable, or how specialization changes consumption possibilities.
concepts.real_world_example: One student may specialize in making presentation slides while another specializes in data analysis, then they trade tasks so both finish a stronger project more quickly.
concepts.graph_connection: The trade-table visual highlights who specializes in what and why both parties can gain after exchange.
concepts.graph_location_text: In the after-trade outcome line showing both sides can consume beyond their no-trade options.
concepts.related_terms: Specialization, Gains from Trade, Comparative Advantage, Opportunity Cost
concepts.quick_recall: Specialize by comparative advantage, then trade at a rate between opportunity costs.

concepts.title: Economic Systems
concepts.short_definition: Economic systems describe how societies decide what to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce.
concepts.full_explanation: A market economy relies heavily on prices, voluntary exchange, private property, and profit incentives. A command economy relies more on central planning and government direction. A mixed economy combines private markets with government rules, taxes, transfers, and public provision. AP Micro usually emphasizes how incentives and prices guide resource allocation, but it also expects you to recognize that real economies blend market and government decision-making.
concepts.why_it_matters: This topic explains the institutional setting behind incentives, private property, and government roles that appear throughout the course.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks how incentives affect decisions, how resources are allocated, or how market and government roles differ.
concepts.real_world_example: A mixed economy may let private firms decide what smartphones to produce while the government still provides public schools, regulates pollution, and collects taxes to fund roads.
concepts.graph_connection: This topic is more comparison-based than graph-based, so the app emphasizes examples and structured explanation instead of a crowded graph.
concepts.related_terms: Economic System, Market Economy, Command Economy, Mixed Economy, Incentives
concepts.quick_recall: Market uses prices, command uses planning, mixed uses both.

concepts.title: Market Equilibrium
concepts.short_definition: The market outcome where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
concepts.full_explanation: Market equilibrium is the benchmark for AP Micro graph analysis because it shows the price and quantity the market settles on when buyers and sellers are both satisfied with the amount traded. When something shifts demand or supply, AP questions usually ask you to compare the old equilibrium with the new one and explain what happened to price, quantity, and total surplus.
concepts.why_it_matters: Almost every Unit 2 graph starts here, and policy graphs measure how far the market moves away from this benchmark.
concepts.exam_use: Use equilibrium to identify the starting point before analyzing shortages, surpluses, taxes, subsidies, or welfare changes.
concepts.real_world_example: If a concert ticket market clears at $80 with 1,000 tickets sold, that price and quantity are the equilibrium outcome for that event.
concepts.graph_connection: On the standard supply-and-demand graph, equilibrium is the intersection of the demand and supply curves. Shifts move the intersection; price controls prevent the market from reaching it.
concepts.graph_location_text: At the intersection of demand and supply, where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
concepts.related_terms: Market Equilibrium, Consumer Surplus, Producer Surplus, Shortage, Surplus
concepts.related_formulas: Total Revenue, Deadweight Loss
concepts.quick_recall: Find the intersection first, then compare what changed after any shift or policy.

concepts.title: Elasticity
concepts.short_definition: A measure of how responsive quantity is to a change in price, income, or another variable.
concepts.full_explanation: Elasticity tells you how strongly buyers or sellers react when conditions change. AP Micro uses it to classify demand or supply as elastic, inelastic, or unit elastic and then connect that result to tax incidence, revenue changes, and market responsiveness. The midpoint method matters because it gives the same elasticity value regardless of direction across the same two points.
concepts.why_it_matters: Elasticity is one of the fastest ways AP questions connect formulas to intuition, especially for tax burden and total revenue.
concepts.exam_use: Use elasticity when AP asks you to calculate responsiveness, compare two markets, or explain who bears more of a tax.
concepts.real_world_example: Gasoline demand is often relatively inelastic in the short run because commuters still need to drive even after price rises.
concepts.graph_connection: Elasticity is interpreted on a demand or supply graph by thinking about how much quantity changes relative to price. Flatter curves are more elastic and steeper curves are more inelastic.
concepts.graph_location_text: The downward-sloping demand curve showing buyers' willingness to buy at each price.
concepts.related_terms: Tax Incidence, Normal Good, Inferior Good, Consumer Surplus
concepts.related_formulas: Price Elasticity of Demand, Price Elasticity of Supply, Cross-Price Elasticity, Income Elasticity, Midpoint Elasticity, Total Revenue
concepts.related_formula_ids_csv: ped, pes, cross-elasticity, income-elasticity, midpoint-elasticity, total-revenue
concepts.quick_recall: More responsive means more elastic; less elastic sides of the market bear more tax burden.

concepts.title: Tax Incidence
concepts.short_definition: How the burden of a tax is split between buyers and sellers.
concepts.full_explanation: Tax incidence is about who actually loses more from a tax after the market adjusts, not just who writes the check to the government. A tax creates a wedge between the buyer price and the seller price. The less elastic side of the market has fewer alternatives, so it absorbs more of that wedge in the form of a worse after-tax outcome.
concepts.why_it_matters: This idea turns elasticity from a definition into a policy-analysis tool, which is exactly how AP frequently tests it.
concepts.exam_use: Use tax incidence when the FRQ asks which side bears more of a tax or how a tax changes buyer price, seller price, and quantity.
concepts.real_world_example: If cigarette demand is very inelastic, smokers may bear most of a cigarette tax through higher prices.
concepts.graph_connection: On the tax graph, compare the vertical distance from the original equilibrium to buyer price and seller price. The side with less elasticity gets hit harder.
concepts.graph_location_text: On the tax graph, in the vertical wedge between the buyer price and seller price after supply shifts upward.
concepts.related_terms: Tax Incidence, Deadweight Loss, Consumer Surplus, Producer Surplus
concepts.related_formulas: Tax Revenue, Deadweight Loss, Price Elasticity of Demand, Price Elasticity of Supply
concepts.quick_recall: Legal burden is not the same thing as economic burden.

concepts.title: Diminishing Marginal Returns
concepts.short_definition: Adding more variable input eventually increases output by smaller and smaller amounts.
concepts.full_explanation: In the short run, at least one input is fixed. As more units of a variable input like labor are added, workers eventually have less fixed capital or workspace per person, so each additional worker adds less output than the previous worker. This is the bridge between production theory and cost theory, because falling marginal product implies rising marginal cost.
concepts.why_it_matters: It explains why firm cost curves take their familiar AP shape instead of staying flat forever.
concepts.exam_use: Use it to explain why marginal product falls, why marginal cost rises, and why short-run production cannot scale efficiently forever.
concepts.real_world_example: A small kitchen gains a lot from adding a second cook, but not much from adding an eighth cook with the same ovens and counter space.
concepts.graph_connection: On the product graph, marginal product peaks and then falls. On the cost graph, that same logic shows up as a rising marginal cost curve.
concepts.graph_location_text: At the point on the production graph where marginal product stops rising and begins to fall.
concepts.related_terms: Diminishing Marginal Returns, Marginal Cost, Average Total Cost
concepts.related_formulas: Marginal Cost
concepts.quick_recall: When each extra worker adds less output, each extra unit becomes more expensive to produce.

concepts.title: Perfect Competition
concepts.short_definition: A market structure with many firms, identical products, easy entry, and no pricing power for individual firms.
concepts.full_explanation: In perfect competition, each individual firm is too small to affect the market price, so it takes price as given. That means its demand curve is horizontal and identical to marginal revenue and average revenue. The firm still uses MR = MC to choose output, but profit or loss depends on comparing market price with ATC, and shutdown depends on comparing price with AVC.
concepts.why_it_matters: Perfect competition is the AP benchmark for efficiency and for comparing how monopoly and other structures create inefficiency.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks about profit maximization, shutdown, long-run equilibrium, or why firms are price takers.
concepts.real_world_example: A textbook wheat farmer example works because one farmer's output is tiny relative to the whole market and buyers see one farmer's wheat as identical to another's.
concepts.graph_connection: On the firm graph, the price line is horizontal and intersects MC at the profit-maximizing quantity. Price compared with ATC shows profit, and price compared with AVC shows shutdown.
concepts.graph_location_text: On the horizontal price = MR = AR line faced by a competitive firm.
concepts.related_terms: Normal Profit, Shutdown Rule, Marginal Cost, Average Total Cost
concepts.related_formulas: Marginal Revenue Basics, Economic Profit, Average Cost Family, Marginal Cost
concepts.quick_recall: For the firm: P = MR = AR, then solve output where MR = MC.

concepts.title: Monopoly
concepts.short_definition: A market structure with one seller, strong barriers to entry, and price-setting power.
concepts.full_explanation: A monopoly faces the market demand curve, so selling more output requires lowering price on all units. That pushes marginal revenue below demand. The monopolist still maximizes profit by using MR = MC for quantity, but then must move up to demand to find price. Because price exceeds marginal cost and output is restricted below the competitive benchmark, monopoly creates allocative inefficiency and deadweight loss.
concepts.why_it_matters: Monopoly is the core benchmark for Unit 4 because it shows how market power changes output, price, profit, and consumer welfare.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks for monopoly price, quantity, profit, price-maker behavior, deadweight loss, or comparison with perfect competition.
concepts.real_world_example: A patented drug producer can restrict output below the competitive level and charge a higher price because competitors are blocked from entering.
concepts.graph_connection: On the monopoly graph, MR lies below demand, MC cuts MR at the chosen quantity, and the price is found above that point on demand.
concepts.graph_location_text: At the quantity where MR intersects MC, then projected down to the horizontal axis.
concepts.related_terms: Monopoly, Marginal Revenue, Price Maker, Barriers to Entry, Price Discrimination
concepts.related_formulas: Imperfect Competition Profit Rule, Marginal Revenue Basics, Economic Profit, Deadweight Loss, Total Revenue
concepts.quick_recall: One seller, barriers to entry, MR = MC for Q, then demand for P.

concepts.title: Oligopoly
concepts.short_definition: A market structure with a few interdependent firms whose decisions depend on expected rival reactions.
concepts.full_explanation: Oligopoly is defined by interdependence. Because only a few firms dominate the market, each firm's pricing, advertising, or output decision affects the payoff to rivals. That is why AP Micro uses game theory, payoff matrices, and sometimes the kinked-demand model to explain oligopoly behavior instead of ordinary competitive equilibrium alone. Oligopoly can behave more competitively or more collusively depending on incentives and enforcement.
concepts.why_it_matters: It explains why some Unit 4 questions are about strategy, incentives, and stability instead of only graph reading.
concepts.exam_use: Use it for payoff-matrix questions, kinked-demand interpretation, collusion analysis, and comparison with monopoly or monopolistic competition.
concepts.real_world_example: Airlines, cell-phone carriers, and major soft-drink producers often watch rival actions closely because only a few firms dominate the market.
concepts.graph_connection: Oligopoly can be shown with a kinked-demand graph for price rigidity or with a game-theory matrix for strategic behavior.
concepts.graph_location_text: On the demand curve with a visible kink at the current price-output point.
concepts.related_terms: Oligopoly, Game Theory, Nash Equilibrium, Collusion, Cartel
concepts.related_formulas: Imperfect Competition Profit Rule, Marginal Revenue Basics
concepts.quick_recall: Few firms means strategic interdependence.

concepts.title: Monopolistic Competition
concepts.short_definition: Many firms sell differentiated products, giving each firm some market power but low barriers to entry.
concepts.full_explanation: Monopolistic competition mixes elements of competition and monopoly. Firms face downward-sloping demand because products are differentiated, so each firm has some price-setting power. In the short run, the firm uses MR = MC and may earn economic profit or loss. In the long run, entry and exit shift demand until price equals ATC, leaving zero economic profit but still not reaching minimum ATC. That is why monopolistic competition has excess capacity and productive inefficiency.
concepts.why_it_matters: It is the main Unit 4 comparison point showing that zero long-run economic profit does not guarantee efficiency.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks about long-run equilibrium, excess capacity, or differences from perfect competition and monopoly.
concepts.real_world_example: Restaurants and clothing brands fit this model because many firms compete while still differentiating their products.
concepts.graph_connection: On the graph, demand lies above MR, the firm chooses output where MR = MC, and long-run demand becomes tangent to ATC at the chosen quantity.
concepts.graph_location_text: In the gap between the firm's chosen output and the lower output that would minimize ATC.
concepts.related_terms: Monopolistic Competition, Excess Capacity, Productive Inefficiency, Price Maker
concepts.related_formulas: Imperfect Competition Profit Rule, Efficiency in Imperfect Competition, Economic Profit
concepts.quick_recall: Short run can have profit; long run has zero economic profit but still excess capacity.

concepts.title: Collusion
concepts.short_definition: Firms cooperate on price or output in order to raise joint profit.
concepts.full_explanation: Collusion happens when firms coordinate output, price, or market sharing instead of competing independently. If collusion succeeds, firms can mimic the monopoly outcome by restricting output and charging a higher price. AP questions usually emphasize that collusion is unstable because each firm has an incentive to cheat on the agreement to gain market share while others hold the line.
concepts.why_it_matters: It connects oligopoly strategy to monopoly-style consumer harm and higher producer profit.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks why firms may try to act like a monopoly, why cartels are unstable, or how consumer welfare changes under coordinated pricing.
concepts.real_world_example: OPEC-style output agreements are the classic AP example of attempted collusion or cartel behavior.
concepts.graph_connection: When firms collude successfully, the monopoly graph is the best visual shorthand because the group behaves like a single monopolist.
concepts.graph_location_text: The downward-sloping demand curve showing buyers' willingness to buy at each price.
concepts.related_terms: Collusion, Cartel, Oligopoly, Prisoner's Dilemma
concepts.related_formulas: Imperfect Competition Profit Rule, Total Revenue
concepts.quick_recall: Collusion aims for monopoly profit, but cheating incentives make it fragile.

concepts.title: Game Theory
concepts.short_definition: A framework for analyzing strategy when each firm's payoff depends on rival choices.
concepts.full_explanation: Game theory studies strategic behavior in oligopoly. Each firm's best move depends on what it expects rivals to do. AP Micro focuses on dominant strategy, Nash equilibrium, and prisoner's dilemma logic. The key lesson is that individually rational behavior can produce an outcome that is worse for firms together than the collusive outcome would have been.
concepts.why_it_matters: It is the reason oligopoly questions often use payoff matrices instead of only cost-and-revenue graphs.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks you to identify a dominant strategy, find the Nash equilibrium, or explain why collusion may collapse.
concepts.real_world_example: Two competing airlines may both cut fares because each fears losing passengers if it keeps fares high while the rival cuts them.
concepts.graph_connection: The payoff matrix is the visual tool for game theory because it compares strategic outcomes across rival choices.
concepts.graph_location_text: In the payoff-matrix cell where neither player wants to change strategy alone.
concepts.related_terms: Game Theory, Dominant Strategy, Nash Equilibrium, Prisoner's Dilemma
concepts.related_formulas: Total Revenue
concepts.quick_recall: Best response logic determines the equilibrium.

concepts.title: Barriers to Entry
concepts.short_definition: Obstacles that keep new firms from entering a market and competing away profit.
concepts.full_explanation: Barriers to entry include legal restrictions, control of key resources, patents, network effects, and very high fixed costs. They matter because they help monopoly and oligopoly profit persist over time. Without barriers, entry would push the market toward more competition and reduce market power. The absence of strong barriers is one reason monopolistic competition ends with zero long-run economic profit.
concepts.why_it_matters: This is the structural reason market power can last instead of disappearing through entry.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks why monopoly can persist, why some industries are concentrated, or how market structures differ in the long run.
concepts.real_world_example: A patented medicine or a local water system with huge infrastructure costs can keep new firms from entering.
concepts.graph_connection: Barriers to entry are not a separate curve, but they explain why the monopoly graph remains relevant in the long run.
concepts.graph_location_text: The downward-sloping demand curve showing buyers' willingness to buy at each price.
concepts.related_terms: Barriers to Entry, Natural Monopoly, Monopoly, Oligopoly
concepts.related_formulas: Efficiency in Imperfect Competition
concepts.quick_recall: Barriers protect market power from entry.

concepts.title: Price Discrimination
concepts.short_definition: Charging different prices to different buyers for the same product when costs are similar.
concepts.full_explanation: Price discrimination lets a firm with market power charge higher prices to buyers with less elastic demand and lower prices to buyers with more elastic demand. To work, the firm must have market power, be able to separate markets, and prevent easy resale. The goal is to capture more consumer surplus and raise profit compared with using one uniform price.
concepts.why_it_matters: It shows one more way market power changes consumer surplus and firm profit beyond the basic monopoly graph.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks when price discrimination is possible, how it affects profit, or why firms charge different groups different prices.
concepts.real_world_example: Airlines charging different fares to business travelers and vacation travelers is a common real-world example.
concepts.graph_connection: Price discrimination is explained using monopoly logic: the firm uses market power to charge different points along different demand conditions.
concepts.graph_location_text: The downward-sloping demand curve showing buyers' willingness to buy at each price.
concepts.related_terms: Price Discrimination, Monopoly, Price Maker, Marginal Revenue
concepts.related_formulas: Imperfect Competition Profit Rule, Total Revenue
concepts.quick_recall: Market power plus separate groups plus limited resale makes price discrimination possible.

concepts.title: Derived Demand
concepts.short_definition: Demand for labor depends on the demand for the output that labor helps produce.
concepts.full_explanation: Derived demand means firms do not hire workers because labor is valuable by itself. They hire workers because those workers help produce goods or services that can be sold. That is why labor demand shifts when product demand changes, when worker productivity changes, or when the firm's marginal revenue changes. In AP Micro, this idea explains why labor demand is tied to the marginal revenue product curve.
concepts.why_it_matters: It explains why Unit 5 is not separate from earlier units: product-market demand and productivity changes spill into labor-market outcomes.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks why labor demand shifts, why MRP changes, or how a change in output demand affects wages and employment.
concepts.real_world_example: If demand for delivery services rises during the holidays, firms demand more drivers because each driver now helps generate more revenue.
concepts.graph_connection: On the competitive labor-market graph, derived demand is the labor-demand or MRP curve. A rise in output demand shifts that curve to the right.
concepts.graph_location_text: On the downward-sloping labor-demand curve.
concepts.related_terms: Derived Demand, Labor Demand, Demand for Labor, Marginal Revenue Product, Resource Demand Shifters
concepts.related_formulas: Marginal Revenue Product
concepts.quick_recall: If the product becomes more valuable, workers become more valuable too.

concepts.title: Competitive Labor Market
concepts.short_definition: A labor market where many firms hire labor and many workers supply labor, so the wage is set by market equilibrium.
concepts.full_explanation: In a competitive labor market, no single employer or worker can control the wage. The market wage is determined by the intersection of labor demand and labor supply. Individual firms are wage takers, so they can hire as much labor as they want at that wage. That is why the firm's hiring rule becomes MRP = wage in a competitive labor market.
concepts.why_it_matters: This is the benchmark Unit 5 outcome that AP questions compare with monopsony, minimum wage, or changes in productivity.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks for equilibrium wage, equilibrium quantity of labor, or the effects of labor-demand and labor-supply shifts.
concepts.real_world_example: A large metro-area market for restaurant servers is closer to competitive because many employers and many workers interact.
concepts.graph_connection: On the labor-market graph, the equilibrium wage and equilibrium quantity of labor come from the intersection of labor demand and labor supply.
concepts.graph_location_text: At the intersection of labor demand and labor supply.
concepts.related_terms: Competitive Labor Market, Equilibrium Wage, Equilibrium Quantity of Labor, Labor Market Equilibrium
concepts.related_formulas: Hiring Rule for Labor, Marginal Revenue Product
concepts.quick_recall: Market graph sets wage; firm takes wage as given.

concepts.title: Hiring Rule: MRP = MRC
concepts.short_definition: A firm hires labor up to the point where marginal revenue product equals marginal resource cost.
concepts.full_explanation: The hiring rule is the factor-market version of marginal analysis. A firm should keep hiring workers as long as the extra revenue from the last worker exceeds the extra cost of that worker. Once MRP falls to MRC, the firm has reached the profit-maximizing quantity of labor. In a competitive labor market, MRC is just the wage, while in monopsony MRC lies above the labor-supply curve.
concepts.why_it_matters: It is the core rule that connects labor-market graphs, firm behavior, and factor-market calculations.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks whether a firm should hire more labor, less labor, or stay at the current employment level.
concepts.real_world_example: If another cashier adds $55 to store revenue but costs $40 per shift hour, the firm benefits from hiring that cashier.
concepts.graph_connection: On the hiring graph, the profit-maximizing quantity of labor is where the downward-sloping MRP curve meets the wage = MRC line.
concepts.graph_location_text: At the employment level where MRP meets MRC.
concepts.related_terms: Hiring Rule, Profit-Maximizing Quantity of Labor, Marginal Revenue Product, Marginal Resource Cost
concepts.related_formulas: Hiring Rule for Labor, Marginal Revenue Product
concepts.quick_recall: MRP > MRC: hire more. MRP < MRC: hire less.

concepts.title: Wage Determination
concepts.short_definition: Wages are determined by labor demand and labor supply in competition, but buyer power can push wages below that benchmark.
concepts.full_explanation: Wage determination depends on both sides of the labor market. Labor demand reflects derived demand and MRP, so it shifts with productivity and product demand. Labor supply reflects worker decisions, population, training, and preferences. In a competitive labor market, the equilibrium wage comes from the intersection of those curves. In monopsony, the wage paid is below the competitive wage because the buyer chooses employment first where MRP equals MRC and then reads wage from the supply curve.
concepts.why_it_matters: It ties together graph interpretation, comparative statics, and the competitive-versus-monopsony comparison.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks what happens to wages after a productivity change, a labor-supply change, or buyer power in the labor market.
concepts.real_world_example: If a town gets a new factory that needs skilled machinists, labor demand rises and wages for machinists tend to increase.
concepts.graph_connection: The labor-market graph shows competitive wage determination, while the monopsony graph shows how buyer power pulls wage below the competitive benchmark.
concepts.graph_location_text: On the vertical axis at the wage read from the labor-market intersection.
concepts.related_terms: Wage Determination, Equilibrium Wage, Labor Supply, Labor Demand, Monopsony
concepts.related_formulas: Hiring Rule for Labor, Marginal Revenue Product
concepts.quick_recall: Say which curve moved, then state what happened to wage and labor hired.

concepts.title: Monopsony
concepts.short_definition: A labor or factor market with a single buyer that has buying power.
concepts.full_explanation: A monopsonist faces an upward-sloping labor supply curve, so hiring an additional worker usually requires raising wages. Because that higher wage often must be paid on earlier workers too, marginal factor cost or marginal resource cost lies above labor supply. The monopsonist hires where MRP equals MRC, then goes down to the supply curve to read the wage, producing lower employment and lower wages than a competitive labor market.
concepts.why_it_matters: Monopsony is a major AP comparison because it mirrors monopoly logic on the buying side of the market.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks how employer market power changes wages and labor hired relative to competition.
concepts.real_world_example: A company town with only one major employer can pay lower wages because workers have few alternative buyers of their labor nearby.
concepts.graph_connection: On the monopsony graph, MRC is above labor supply, hiring occurs where MRP = MRC, and wage is read from labor supply at that quantity.
concepts.graph_location_text: On the MFC curve above labor supply; hiring occurs where MRP meets MFC and wage is read from labor supply at that quantity.
concepts.related_terms: Monopsony, Marginal Resource Cost, Marginal Factor Cost, Marginal Revenue Product, Competitive Labor Market
concepts.related_formulas: Marginal Revenue Product, Hiring Rule for Labor
concepts.quick_recall: Hire where MRP = MRC, then read wage from supply, not from MRC.

concepts.title: Allocative and Productive Efficiency
concepts.short_definition: Allocative efficiency means producing the amount society values most; productive efficiency means producing at the lowest possible cost.
concepts.full_explanation: Allocative efficiency happens when price equals marginal cost, meaning the last unit produced is worth exactly what it costs to society. Productive efficiency happens when output is produced at the minimum average total cost. AP Micro compares market structures using these ideas because perfect competition in long-run equilibrium achieves both, while monopoly and monopolistic competition do not.
concepts.why_it_matters: These efficiency ideas tie together welfare, market structure comparisons, and graph reading.
concepts.exam_use: Use them when AP asks whether a market is socially efficient, whether a firm produces at minimum ATC, or how a policy changes welfare.
concepts.real_world_example: A competitive market tends to produce closer to the efficient quantity than a monopoly that restricts output and raises price.
concepts.graph_connection: On a firm or welfare graph, allocative efficiency is tied to P = MC. Productive efficiency is tied to output at minimum ATC.
concepts.graph_location_text: Allocative efficiency appears where price or MSB equals marginal cost, while productive efficiency is at the minimum point of ATC.
concepts.related_terms: Deadweight Loss, Average Total Cost, Marginal Cost, Normal Profit
concepts.related_formulas: Deadweight Loss, Average Cost Family, Marginal Cost
concepts.quick_recall: Allocative = P = MC. Productive = minimum ATC.

concepts.title: Negative Externalities
concepts.short_definition: A market activity imposes outside costs on third parties, so the private market produces too much.
concepts.full_explanation: Negative externalities create an external cost that market participants do not fully count. That means marginal private cost is below marginal social cost, so the market quantity is larger than the socially optimal quantity. On the AP graph, the private market settles where MPC meets MSB, but the socially efficient outcome is where MSC meets MSB. The difference between those quantities creates deadweight loss because the market is producing units whose full social cost exceeds their social benefit.
concepts.why_it_matters: This is one of the clearest AP examples of market failure because the market equilibrium is not socially efficient once outside costs are included.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks you to identify overproduction, label MPC and MSC, find the socially optimal quantity, explain deadweight loss, or justify a corrective tax or regulation.
concepts.real_world_example: A factory that pollutes a river imposes cleanup and health costs on nearby households who were not part of the sale.
concepts.graph_connection: On the externality graph, Qm is where MPC meets MSB, Qsoc is where MSC meets MSB, and the vertical gap between MSC and MPC captures the external cost.
concepts.graph_location_text: On the negative externality graph, MSC lies above MPC, Qm is where MPC meets MSB, and Qsoc is where MSC meets MSB.
concepts.related_terms: Externality, Negative Externality, MPC, MSC, Social Cost, Socially Optimal Quantity, Corrective Tax, Deadweight Loss
concepts.related_vocab_ids_csv: externality, negative-externality, mpc, msc, social-cost, socially-optimal-quantity, corrective-tax, deadweight-loss
concepts.related_formulas: Deadweight Loss
concepts.quick_recall: Negative externality = external cost, MSC above MPC, market overproduces, corrective tax moves Q left.

concepts.title: Positive Externalities
concepts.short_definition: A market activity creates outside benefits, so the private market produces too little.
concepts.full_explanation: Positive externalities create an external benefit that the private market does not fully count. That means marginal private benefit is below marginal social benefit, so the market quantity is smaller than the socially optimal quantity. On the AP graph, the private market settles where MPB meets MSC, but the socially efficient outcome is where MSB meets MSC. The missing units between those quantities create deadweight loss because society values them more than their social cost.
concepts.why_it_matters: This shows why markets can underprovide goods such as education or vaccinations even when those goods generate broader social gains.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks you to identify underproduction, label MPB and MSB, find the socially optimal quantity, explain deadweight loss, or justify a corrective subsidy or public provision.
concepts.real_world_example: A vaccination benefits the person getting it and also reduces disease spread to others.
concepts.graph_connection: On the externality graph, Qm is where MPB meets MSC, Qsoc is where MSB meets MSC, and the vertical gap between MSB and MPB captures the external benefit.
concepts.graph_location_text: On the positive externality graph, MSB lies above MPB, Qm is where MPB meets MSC, and Qsoc is where MSB meets MSC.
concepts.related_terms: Externality, Positive Externality, MPB, MSB, Social Benefit, Socially Optimal Quantity, Subsidy, Deadweight Loss
concepts.related_vocab_ids_csv: externality, positive-externality, mpb, msb, social-benefit, socially-optimal-quantity, subsidy, deadweight-loss
concepts.related_formulas: Deadweight Loss
concepts.quick_recall: Positive externality = external benefit, MSB above MPB, market underproduces, subsidy moves Q right.

concepts.title: Public Goods and Free Rider
concepts.short_definition: Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable, and the free-rider problem makes private markets underprovide them.
concepts.full_explanation: A public good can be used by many people at once and it is hard to exclude nonpayers, so private sellers struggle to charge everyone who benefits. That creates the free-rider problem: people can wait for others to pay and still receive the service. As a result, the private market usually provides too little of the good relative to the socially efficient amount.
concepts.why_it_matters: This is one of the clearest AP Micro examples of why markets can fail even when buyers value the good.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks you to classify a good, explain why private provision is too low, or justify taxation or public provision.
concepts.real_world_example: National defense and street lighting are classic examples because many people benefit at once and excluding nonpayers is difficult.
concepts.graph_connection: The app uses a simple classification visual that links public goods to free-rider underprovision rather than a standard supply-demand graph.
concepts.graph_location_text: In the left panel of the public-goods/common-resources visual, where the good is classified as non-rival and non-excludable.
concepts.related_terms: Public Good, Free Rider, Free Rider Problem, Social Benefit
concepts.related_formulas: Deadweight Loss
concepts.quick_recall: Public good = non-rival + non-excludable, so free riders make private provision too low.

concepts.title: Common Resources
concepts.short_definition: A common resource is rival and non-excludable, so open access tends to cause overuse.
concepts.full_explanation: Common resources differ from public goods because they are rival in consumption: when one user consumes more, less is available for others. At the same time, they are non-excludable, so it is hard to stop users from accessing them. This combination creates overuse because each individual user considers private benefit but ignores the depletion or congestion cost imposed on everyone else. That logic is why common resources often resemble a negative-externality problem in AP Micro.
concepts.why_it_matters: This category explains why fisheries, grazing land, and other open-access resources can be used beyond the socially efficient amount.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks you to classify a good, explain overuse, or justify quotas, permits, regulation, or property rights.
concepts.real_world_example: An open-access fishery is vulnerable to overfishing because each fishing boat has an incentive to catch more before someone else does.
concepts.graph_connection: The reference visual links common-resource overuse to the same social-cost logic found on a negative externality graph.
concepts.graph_location_text: In the right panel of the public-goods/common-resources visual, where the resource is classified as rival and non-excludable.
concepts.related_terms: Common Resource, Tragedy of the Commons, Regulation, Negative Externality, Social Cost
concepts.related_formulas: Deadweight Loss
concepts.quick_recall: Common resource = rival + non-excludable, so private use tends to overshoot the efficient amount.

concepts.title: Free Rider Problem
concepts.short_definition: The free-rider problem occurs when people can benefit from a good without paying for it.
concepts.full_explanation: A free rider is someone who enjoys a benefit without contributing to the cost. When many people behave that way, the private market sees less willingness to pay than the good's full social benefit would justify. That is why public goods are underprovided in private markets. The free-rider problem is not about overuse of a resource; it is about too little private provision because sellers cannot reliably charge all beneficiaries.
concepts.why_it_matters: This is the key logic connecting public goods to government provision and taxation on AP Micro exams.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks why a private market may fail to provide enough of a public good or why government financing can increase efficiency.
concepts.real_world_example: A neighborhood resident may enjoy street lighting even if that resident refuses to contribute voluntarily to paying for it.
concepts.graph_connection: The public-good panel highlights how private willingness to pay can understate total social benefit when nonpayers still receive the service.
concepts.graph_location_text: In the public-good panel, where private willingness to pay is shown as too low because nonpayers still benefit.
concepts.related_terms: Free Rider, Free Rider Problem, Public Good, Social Benefit
concepts.related_formulas: Deadweight Loss
concepts.quick_recall: Free rider problem = people can benefit without paying, so private supply is too low.

concepts.title: Government Intervention and Corrective Policy
concepts.short_definition: Government intervention aims to move market outcomes toward the socially efficient outcome when private incentives diverge from social costs or benefits.
concepts.full_explanation: Corrective policy in Unit 6 is about internalizing external costs or external benefits. A corrective tax is the standard tool for negative externalities because it pushes private decision-makers to account for the outside cost. A subsidy is the standard tool for positive externalities because it raises private incentive to produce or consume a good with outside benefits. Regulation, quotas, permits, and public provision can also improve outcomes when direct pricing tools are not enough or when AP asks for another policy path. The key policy test is always the same: does the intervention move quantity toward MSB = MSC?
concepts.why_it_matters: This turns Unit 6 from pure diagnosis into policy analysis, which is exactly how many AP free-response questions are framed.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks which policy fits a negative or positive externality, how policy changes the graph, or why government may provide public goods directly.
concepts.real_world_example: A pollution tax reduces emissions, a vaccine subsidy raises immunization rates, and public funding for street lighting solves a free-rider problem.
concepts.graph_connection: On externality graphs, policy is judged by whether it moves the market quantity toward the socially optimal quantity and shrinks deadweight loss.
concepts.graph_location_text: On externality graphs, policy is the move from the private-market quantity toward the socially optimal quantity where MSB = MSC.
concepts.related_terms: Corrective Tax, Subsidy, Regulation, Socially Optimal Quantity, Socially Efficient Outcome, Public Good, Common Resource
concepts.related_vocab_ids_csv: corrective-tax, subsidy, regulation, socially-optimal-quantity, socially-efficient-outcome, public-good, common-resource
concepts.related_formulas: Deadweight Loss
concepts.quick_recall: Negative externality -> tax or regulation. Positive externality -> subsidy or public support. Goal = move Q toward MSB = MSC.

concepts.title: Tragedy of the Commons
concepts.short_definition: The tragedy of the commons is the overuse of a common resource because each user ignores the cost imposed on others.
concepts.full_explanation: When access to a rival resource is open, each person has an incentive to use more before others do. But each user's decision reduces what remains for everyone else. Because that depletion cost is spread across other users, no one person has a strong incentive to conserve on behalf of the group. The result is overuse relative to the socially efficient outcome. That is why the tragedy of the commons is best understood as a common-resource version of external-cost logic.
concepts.why_it_matters: It is the AP Micro bridge between classification language and policy solutions such as quotas, regulation, permits, and property rights.
concepts.exam_use: Use it when AP asks why a common resource is overused or how policy can reduce overfishing, congestion, or overgrazing.
concepts.real_world_example: If each rancher adds another cow to shared grazing land, the field can become overgrazed even though each rancher acted in self-interest.
concepts.graph_connection: The common-resource panel emphasizes overuse, while the negative externality graph provides the welfare logic behind why too much use is inefficient.
concepts.graph_location_text: In the common-resource panel as the overuse outcome, reinforced by the negative-externality logic of producing beyond the socially efficient amount.
concepts.related_terms: Common Resource, Tragedy of the Commons, Regulation, Social Cost, Socially Efficient Outcome
concepts.related_formulas: Deadweight Loss
concepts.quick_recall: Open access + rivalry = overuse unless rules or ownership restrain it.

quick_review.title: Unit 1 Foundations
quick_review.body: Scarcity forces choice. Every choice has an opportunity cost. PPC points on the curve are efficient, inside are inefficient, and outside are unattainable. Comparative advantage uses lower opportunity cost, not higher output. Specialization and trade create gains when terms of trade fall between opportunity costs.

quick_review.title: Market Structures Snapshot
quick_review.body: Perfect competition: many firms, identical product, price taker, P = MR, efficient in long run. Monopoly: one firm, barriers to entry, price maker, P > MR, output restricted, deadweight loss. Monopolistic competition: many firms, differentiated products, some price control, zero long-run economic profit, excess capacity. Oligopoly: few interdependent firms, strategic behavior matters, and game theory explains pricing incentives.

quick_review.title: Elasticity Cues
quick_review.body: Many substitutes, luxury status, large budget share, and long adjustment time usually make demand more elastic. Few substitutes, necessity status, small budget share, and short adjustment time make it more inelastic. Less elastic side of the market bears more tax burden.

quick_review.title: Cost Curve Cues
quick_review.body: MC cuts AVC and ATC at their minimums. If MC is below an average curve, the average falls. If MC is above, the average rises. Fixed cost changes shift AFC and ATC, but not MC.

quick_review.title: Welfare and DWL Cues
quick_review.body: Competitive equilibrium maximizes total surplus when there are no externalities. Taxes, subsidies, price controls, monopoly power, and externalities all create deadweight loss by moving quantity away from the efficient outcome.

quick_review.title: If You See This, Think This
quick_review.body: MR = MC: profit-max quantity. Go up to demand: monopoly price. P < AVC: short-run shutdown. P = ATC: zero economic profit. MSB = MSC: social optimum. Lower opportunity cost: comparative advantage. Less elastic side: larger tax burden.

quick_review.title: Exam Reminders
quick_review.body: Label axes before analyzing a graph. Say whether a change is a shift or movement along a curve. State whether quantity is above or below the socially efficient level. Use post-policy quantity for area calculations. Read the direction of opportunity cost carefully.

exam_cram.title: High-Yield Terms
exam_cram.body: Opportunity cost, comparative advantage, equilibrium, elasticity, consumer surplus, producer surplus, deadweight loss, marginal cost, normal profit, marginal revenue, monopoly, MRP, externality, public good, common resource.

exam_cram.title: High-Yield Graphs
exam_cram.body: PPC, supply and demand, tax, subsidy, price ceiling, price floor, cost curves, perfect competition firm, monopoly, labor market, negative externality, positive externality, Lorenz curve.

exam_cram.title: High-Yield Formulas
exam_cram.body: Midpoint elasticity, TR = P x Q, MR = delta TR / delta Q, TC = FC + VC, AFC, AVC, ATC, profit = TR - TC, profit = (P - ATC) x Q, DWL = 1/2 x base x height, MRP = MP x MR.

exam_cram.title: High-Yield Policy Reminders
exam_cram.body: Tax lowers quantity. Subsidy raises quantity. Ceiling causes shortage. Floor causes surplus. Corrective tax reduces negative externality. Corrective subsidy raises positive externality. Less elastic side bears more tax burden.

exam_cram.title: High-Yield Market Structure Facts
exam_cram.body: Perfect competition: P = MR. Monopoly: MR = MC for Q, then demand for P. Monopolistic competition: zero long-run economic profit but excess capacity. Oligopoly: interdependence, game theory, and possible collusion. Monopsony: MFC above labor supply.

reference.title: Unit 1 Systems and Trade
reference.body: Market economy: decentralized decisions, private property, strong price incentives. Command economy: central planning and government direction. Mixed economy: market allocation plus government role. Comparative advantage: lower opportunity cost. Absolute advantage: higher total output. Gains from trade: specialize, then trade within opportunity-cost limits.

reference.title: Demand and Supply Shift Triggers
reference.body: Demand shifts with income, tastes, expectations, related goods, and number of buyers. Supply shifts with input costs, technology, taxes/subsidies, expectations, and number of sellers. Price changes never shift the curve they are measured on.

reference.title: Market Structure Table
reference.body: Perfect competition: efficient in long run, no market power, P = MR = MC in equilibrium. Monopoly: price maker, high barriers to entry, underproduces, charges higher price, and creates deadweight loss. Monopolistic competition: differentiated goods, low barriers to entry, zero long-run economic profit, excess capacity, and P > MC. Oligopoly: few firms, strategic interdependence, possible collusion, payoff-matrix logic, and sometimes kinked demand.

reference.title: Policy Effects
reference.body: Tax: quantity down, buyer price up, seller price down. Subsidy: quantity up, buyer price down, seller price up. Price ceiling: shortage. Price floor: surplus. Corrective tax reduces negative externality. Corrective subsidy increases positive externality.

reference.title: Factor Market Rules
reference.body: Hire more inputs when marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost. In competitive labor markets, hire until MRP = wage. In monopsony, hire where MRP = MFC, then read wage from labor supply.

reference.title: Formula Sheet
reference.body: Elasticity midpoint: ((Q2 - Q1) / average Q) / ((P2 - P1) / average P). Total revenue = Price x Quantity. Marginal revenue = change in total revenue / change in quantity. Total cost = fixed cost + variable cost. AFC = FC / Q. AVC = VC / Q. ATC = TC / Q. Profit = total revenue - total cost or (Price - ATC) x Quantity. Deadweight loss = 1/2 x base x height. MRP = marginal product x marginal revenue. Hiring rule: hire until MRP = MRC.

reference.title: Graph ID Guide
reference.body: Core graph families: ppc, trade-table, supply-demand, surplus-welfare, tax, subsidy, price-ceiling, price-floor, cost-curves, perfect-competition, perfect-competition-market, monopoly, monopolistic-competition, kinked-demand, game-theory-matrix, labor-market, hiring-rule, monopsony, production-function, negative-externality, positive-externality, public-goods-common-resources, lorenz. If you need a fast graph lookup, start with the graph list or the revision hub, then jump by title from vocabulary or concept pages.

reference.title: Extra Micro Terms
reference.body: Cross-unit reminders: ceteris paribus means hold other things constant. Explicit cost is a direct out-of-pocket payment. Implicit cost is the opportunity cost of using your own resources. Accounting profit ignores implicit costs; economic profit includes them. Marginal analysis compares one more benefit with one more cost. Allocative efficiency means society gets the right quantity where benefit matches cost. Productive efficiency means producing at the lowest possible average total cost. Tradable permits and property rights are policy tools for market-failure questions. Public provision is a likely response when a public good faces a free-rider problem.

reference.title: Common Mistakes by Unit
reference.body: Unit 1: comparative advantage is lower opportunity cost, not higher output. Unit 2: price changes move along curves, they do not shift the curve being measured. Unit 3: shutdown uses AVC, not ATC. Unit 4: MR = MC gives quantity first, then use demand for price. Unit 5: in monopsony, read wage from labor supply, not MRC. Unit 6: the social optimum is where MSB = MSC, not necessarily the market equilibrium.

reference.title: If You See This, Think This
reference.body: MR = MC: profit-maximizing quantity. Go up to demand: monopoly price. P = MR = AR: perfect-competition firm. P < AVC: shutdown in the short run. P = ATC: zero economic profit. MSB = MSC: socially efficient outcome. MSC above MPC: negative externality and overproduction. MSB above MPB: positive externality and underproduction. Lower opportunity cost: comparative advantage. Less elastic side: bears more of the tax burden.
